einzeln.note: Adjective meaning 'individual, separate' — considered on its own rather than as part of a group. Used attributively before a noun it declines normally; used adverbially it means 'individually, one at a time' and takes no ending. The examples below use the attributive adjective so the declension is fully visible.

nominative.german: Jeder einzelne Teilnehmer bekommt eine Urkunde.
nominative.english: Every single participant receives a certificate.
nominative.hint: Subject of bekommt, so nominative. Jeder is a der-word and already carries the masculine nominative ending -er, so the adjective drops to the weak ending -e: einzelne.

accusative.german: Wir haben jeden einzelnen Fall sorgfältig geprüft.
accusative.english: We checked every single case carefully.
accusative.hint: Direct object of prüfen, so accusative. Jeden shows the masculine accusative -en, mirroring den, and the adjective takes the weak ending -en after it.

dative.german: Der Chef hat mit jedem einzelnen Mitarbeiter gesprochen.
dative.english: The boss spoke with every single employee.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Jedem shows the masculine dative -em, mirroring dem, and the adjective takes the weak -en after it.

genitive.german: Die Prüfung jedes einzelnen Antrags dauert mehrere Wochen.
genitive.english: The examination of every single application takes several weeks.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Prüfung. Three endings appear at once: jedes with the masculine genitive -es, the weak adjective ending -en, and the noun's own genitive -s.

einzeln.proTip: Attributive einzeln declines (der einzelne Fall, dem einzelnen Fall); adverbial einzeln does not (Bitte einzeln eintreten). Keep it apart from einzig, which means 'only, sole' — einzeln is about separateness, einzig about uniqueness. Also note im Einzelnen (in detail).

der Entwurf.note: Masculine noun meaning 'draft, design' (a preliminary version of a document or plan). Nouns decline for case. Entwurf itself only changes form in the genitive singular (des Entwurfs/Entwurfes) and the dative plural (den Entwürfen); in the other singular cases only the article changes. Plural: die Entwürfe.

nominative.german: Der Entwurf liegt schon auf dem Tisch.
nominative.english: The draft is already lying on the table.
nominative.hint: Subject of liegt, so nominative. Der is the masculine nominative article; Entwurf has no ending of its own here.

accusative.german: Der Architekt hat den Entwurf gestern fertig gemacht.
accusative.english: The architect finished the draft yesterday.
accusative.hint: Direct object of fertig machen, so accusative. Only the article changes: masculine der becomes den in the accusative. The noun Entwurf takes no accusative ending.

dative.german: Der Chef stimmte dem Entwurf sofort zu.
dative.english: The boss approved the draft immediately.
dative.hint: Dative required by the verb zustimmen, which always takes a dative object — this is verb government, not a preposition and not an indirect object. Masculine dative article dem; the noun stays Entwurf.

genitive.german: Die Änderungen des Entwurfs sind sehr klein.
genitive.english: The changes to the draft are very small.
genitive.hint: Genitive showing an 'of' relationship to Änderungen. Masculine genitive article des, and the noun itself adds -s (Entwurfes is the equally correct longer form).

der Entwurf.proTip: Entwurf is masculine and forms its plural with an umlaut: Entwürfe. Watch the two places where an ending actually appears on the noun — genitive singular des Entwurfs and dative plural den Entwürfen. Useful collocations: einen Entwurf machen, einen Entwurf vorlegen (to make / to submit a draft).

die Erinnerung.note: Feminine noun meaning 'memory, recollection' (something you remember). Nouns decline for case, but a feminine noun never changes its own form in the singular — all four singular cases are Erinnerung, and only the article or determiner shows the case. Plural: die Erinnerungen.

nominative.german: Diese Erinnerung macht mich immer wieder glücklich.
nominative.english: This memory makes me happy again and again.
nominative.hint: Subject of macht, so nominative. Diese is the feminine nominative form of dieser; the noun Erinnerung carries no ending, since feminine nouns are unchanged in the singular.

accusative.german: Ich habe eine schöne Erinnerung an diesen Sommer.
accusative.english: I have a fond memory of that summer.
accusative.hint: Direct object of habe, so accusative. Feminine eine looks the same in nominative and accusative; schöne takes the mixed-declension ending -e after an ein-word in the feminine accusative. The separate phrase an diesen Sommer is also accusative, governed by an.

dative.german: Mit dieser Erinnerung schlief er endlich ein.
dative.english: With this memory he finally fell asleep.
dative.hint: Dative required by the preposition mit, which always governs the dative. Dieser is the feminine dative form; the noun itself is still Erinnerung.

genitive.german: Die Kraft der Erinnerung überrascht mich oft.
genitive.english: The power of memory often surprises me.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Kraft. The feminine genitive article is der — identical in form to the feminine dative article, so its position directly after the noun Kraft is what marks it as genitive here. Feminine nouns add no genitive -s.

die Erinnerung.proTip: Every German noun ending in -ung is feminine: die Erinnerung, die Zeitung, die Wohnung. The fixed pattern is Erinnerung an + accusative — eine Erinnerung an meine Kindheit (a memory of my childhood).

verstehen.note: Verb meaning 'to understand'. Verbs conjugate; they do not decline for case — they conjugate for person, number and tense (ich verstehe, du verstehst, er verstand, er hat verstanden). What verstehen does is assign case to the nouns around it: its subject is nominative and its object is accusative. The examples below therefore show case on the noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing verstehen.

nominative.german: Der neue Lehrer versteht seine Schüler wirklich gut.
nominative.english: The new teacher really understands his students well.
nominative.hint: Subject of versteht, so nominative — verstehen has no case form itself, but it requires a nominative subject. Masculine nominative article der; neue takes the weak ending -e after the definite article.

accusative.german: Ich verstehe deine Frage leider nicht.
accusative.english: Unfortunately I don't understand your question.
accusative.hint: Direct object of verstehe, so accusative — verstehen is transitive and governs the accusative. Deine is the feminine accusative form of dein (identical to the feminine nominative); Frage is unchanged.

dative.german: Meine Schwester hilft mir, weil ich die Aufgabe nicht verstehe.
dative.english: My sister is helping me because I don't understand the task.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun — but the dative comes from helfen, not from verstehen. Helfen always takes a dative object, while verstehen in the subordinate clause takes the accusative object die Aufgabe.

genitive.german: Der Sinn des Textes ist ohne Wörterbuch schwer zu verstehen.
genitive.english: The meaning of the text is hard to understand without a dictionary.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Sinn; verstehen itself contributes no case and does not require a genitive object here. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -es (Text is a one-syllable noun, so the longer -es is preferred).

verstehen.proTip: Verstehen is a strong verb: verstehen – verstand – hat verstanden, with no vowel change in the present tense. Distinguish the plain transitive use (Ich verstehe dich) from reflexive sich verstehen mit + dative, which means 'to get along with': Ich verstehe mich gut mit meinem Bruder.

dieser / diese / dieses.note: Demonstrative determiner (and pronoun) meaning 'this'. It declines fully for case, gender and number, and it is a der-word: its endings copy those of the definite article der/die/das. An adjective following it therefore takes weak endings.

nominative.german: Dieses Buch gehört meinem kleinen Bruder.
nominative.english: This book belongs to my little brother.
nominative.hint: Subject of gehört, so nominative. Neuter nominative dieses mirrors das; the noun Buch takes no ending. Gehören then sends its own object, meinem kleinen Bruder, into the dative.

accusative.german: Ich nehme diesen schweren Koffer.
accusative.english: I'll take this heavy suitcase.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehme, so accusative. Masculine accusative diesen mirrors den; because the determiner already shows the case, the adjective schweren takes the weak ending -en.

dative.german: Ich gebe diesem Kind einen Apfel.
dative.english: I'm giving this child an apple.
dative.hint: Indirect object of geben, so dative. Neuter dative diesem mirrors dem. The direct object einen Apfel stays accusative — the standard dative-then-accusative pattern with geben.

genitive.german: Der Preis dieses Autos ist einfach zu hoch.
genitive.english: The price of this car is simply too high.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Preis. Neuter genitive dieses mirrors des, and the noun adds the genitive -s: Autos.

dieser / diese / dieses.proTip: Take the endings straight from der/die/das: dieser/diese/dieses, diesen, diesem, dieser, dieses. Watch the form dieses — it is both neuter nominative/accusative (dieses Buch) and masculine/neuter genitive (dieses Autos); the -s on the noun tells you which. The same endings fit jener, jeder, welcher and solcher.

überhaupt.note: Adverb/particle meaning 'at all' (intensifying a negation) or 'in general, on the whole'. Adverbs do not decline for case and überhaupt is invariable — it has no endings in any context and does not govern a case. The sentences below therefore demonstrate each case on other noun or pronoun phrases while containing the target word.

nominative.german: Der Lärm von der Straße stört mich überhaupt nicht.
nominative.english: The noise from the street doesn't bother me at all.
nominative.hint: Subject of stört, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Überhaupt simply strengthens the negation nicht and takes no ending of its own. (Von der Straße is dative, governed by von.)

accusative.german: Ich habe heute überhaupt keinen Hunger.
accusative.english: I'm not hungry at all today.
accusative.hint: Direct object of habe, so accusative. Keinen is the masculine accusative form of kein; überhaupt kein is the standard way to say 'no ... at all', and überhaupt itself stays unchanged.

dative.german: Er hat mir überhaupt nicht geantwortet.
dative.english: He didn't answer me at all.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun required by the verb antworten, which takes a dative object rather than an accusative one. The dative comes from the verb, not from überhaupt.

genitive.german: Überhaupt ist die wirtschaftliche Lage des Landes sehr schwierig.
genitive.english: In general, the economic situation of the country is very difficult.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Lage; neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -es. Here überhaupt opens the sentence in its 'in general' meaning and is still invariable.

überhaupt.proTip: Two clearly different uses: überhaupt nicht / überhaupt kein means 'not at all', while überhaupt at the start of a sentence means 'in general, on the whole'. In a question it can add surprise or doubt: Hast du das überhaupt gelesen? — Did you even read it?

unser.note: Possessive determiner meaning 'our'. It declines for case, gender and number and belongs to the ein-words, so it follows the mixed pattern: no ending in the masculine nominative and the neuter nominative/accusative, and the normal der-word endings everywhere else. Endings attach to the stem unser-.

nominative.german: Unser Hund schläft den ganzen Tag im Garten.
nominative.english: Our dog sleeps in the garden all day long.
nominative.hint: Subject of schläft, so nominative. Masculine nominative is one of the three slots where an ein-word takes no ending, so it is unser, not unserer.

accusative.german: Wir verkaufen unseren alten Wagen.
accusative.english: We're selling our old car.
accusative.hint: Direct object of verkaufen, so accusative. Masculine accusative unseren carries the ending -en; because the determiner already shows the case, the adjective alten takes the weak ending -en too.

dative.german: Wir zeigen unserer Nachbarin die neuen Fotos.
dative.english: We're showing our neighbour the new photos.
dative.hint: Indirect object of zeigen, so dative. Feminine dative adds -er to the stem: unserer. The direct object die neuen Fotos remains accusative.

genitive.german: Das Dach unseres Hauses ist seit letztem Jahr neu.
genitive.english: The roof of our house has been new since last year.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Dach. Neuter genitive adds -es to the determiner (unseres) and the noun also takes -es: Hauses. Both endings are needed.

unser.proTip: Unser already ends in -er as part of its stem, so don't mistake that for an ending — case endings come after it: unseres, unserem, unseren. In speech the middle -e- is often dropped (unsren, unserm), but write the full forms. Euer is its counterpart and does lose the -e- when an ending is added: euer → eure, euren.

gleich.note: Two distinct uses. As an attributive adjective it means 'same, identical' and declines normally (der gleiche Fehler). As an adverb it means 'right away, in a moment' and is invariable, with no ending at all. The examples below all use the adjective so that the declension is visible; the adverb use is covered in the pro-tip.

nominative.german: Der gleiche Fehler passiert mir immer wieder.
nominative.english: The same mistake happens to me again and again.
nominative.hint: Subject of passiert, so nominative. Masculine nominative article der; gleiche takes the weak adjective ending -e because the definite article already marks the case. Mir is a separate dative required by passieren.

accusative.german: Wir haben zufällig den gleichen Zug genommen.
accusative.english: We happened to take the same train.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehmen, so accusative. The article changes from der to den, and the adjective takes the weak ending -en, the regular masculine accusative form after a definite article.

dative.german: Ich wohne in der gleichen Straße wie du.
dative.english: I live on the same street as you.
dative.hint: Dative after the two-way preposition in, because the sentence states a location, not a movement. Feminine dative article der, with the weak adjective ending -en.

genitive.german: Die Mitglieder der gleichen Familie streiten sich oft.
genitive.english: Members of the same family often argue with each other.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Mitglieder. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun Familie adds nothing, since feminine nouns take no genitive -s.

gleich.proTip: Keep the two uses apart: adjective gleich declines (das gleiche Problem), adverb gleich never does (Ich komme gleich — I'm coming right away). Also distinguish der gleiche (the same kind, another one just like it) from derselbe (the very same one).

als.note: A subordinating conjunction ('when', for a single event in the past), a comparison word ('than', after a comparative), and a particle meaning 'as, in the role of'. It is invariable and has no case forms. Importantly, als does not govern a case: after a comparative and in the 'as' sense, the following phrase simply copies the case of the element it relates to.

nominative.german: Mein Bruder ist deutlich größer als ich.
nominative.english: My brother is considerably taller than I am.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative. The pronoun ich after als is also nominative, because it is being compared with the nominative subject — als passes the case through rather than assigning one.

accusative.german: Ich kenne ihn schon viel länger als dich.
accusative.english: I have known him much longer than you.
accusative.hint: Accusative, because it is compared with ihn, the accusative object of kenne. This is the key rule: after a comparative, the item following als takes the same case as the item it is compared with.

dative.german: Als er mir das Geld zurückgab, war ich völlig überrascht.
dative.english: When he gave me the money back, I was completely surprised.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of zurückgeben; das Geld is the accusative direct object. Here als is the conjunction 'when' for a single past event, so it sends the conjugated verb zurückgab to the end of its clause.

genitive.german: Als Vorsitzender des Vereins hielt er eine kurze Rede.
genitive.english: As chairman of the club, he gave a short speech.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Vorsitzender; masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s. Vorsitzender itself is nominative, matching the subject er, because als copies the case rather than assigning one.

als.proTip: Three jobs, three tests. 'Than' after a comparative: größer als. 'When' for one completed past event: Als ich klein war — use wenn for repeated or present events. 'As / in the capacity of': als Lehrer arbeiten. And remember the case after als is inherited, not governed: Er ist älter als ich (nominative), but Ich kenne ihn länger als dich (accusative).

etwa.note: Adverb meaning 'roughly, approximately' before a quantity, or 'for instance' when introducing an example. Adverbs do not decline for case; etwa is completely invariable and never affects the case of the phrase it modifies. The cases below are therefore shown on other phrases in sentences containing etwa.

nominative.german: Etwa zwanzig Gäste waren schon vor dem Konzert da.
nominative.english: Roughly twenty guests were already there before the concert.
nominative.hint: Subject of waren, so nominative plural. Etwa only softens the number zwanzig and takes no ending; Gäste is the umlauted plural of Gast, and the nominative plural adds nothing further.

accusative.german: Die Fahrt nach Hamburg dauert etwa eine Stunde.
accusative.english: The journey to Hamburg takes about an hour.
accusative.hint: Accusative — but an accusative of duration rather than a true direct object, since German puts spans of time in the accusative after verbs like dauern and warten. Feminine eine is identical in the nominative and accusative.

dative.german: Wir treffen uns etwa in einer Woche wieder.
dative.english: We'll meet again in about a week.
dative.hint: Dative required by in when it refers to a point in time; einer is the feminine dative form of ein. Etwa modifies the whole time expression without changing its case.

genitive.german: Etwa die Hälfte der Studenten hat gestern gefehlt.
genitive.english: About half of the students were absent yesterday.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after die Hälfte. The genitive plural article is der for all genders, and Student is a weak (n-) noun, so every form outside the nominative singular is Studenten.

etwa.proTip: Etwa before a number means 'approximately' and is interchangeable with ungefähr and zirka. Meaning 'for instance' it is more formal than zum Beispiel: große Städte wie etwa Berlin. In a question, nicht etwa signals surprise or worry: Du hast doch nicht etwa vergessen?

anderer.note: Adjective meaning 'other, different'. It declines like any ordinary adjective — strong, weak or mixed depending on what precedes it — and is not a der-word. The dictionary form anderer already shows the masculine strong nominative ending; the stem is ander-.

nominative.german: Ein anderer Weg führt direkt zum See.
nominative.english: Another path leads directly to the lake.
nominative.hint: Subject of führt, so nominative. This is mixed declension: ein has no ending in the masculine nominative, so the adjective must show the case itself with the strong ending -er — anderer.

accusative.german: Ich suche einen anderen Stuhl für das Büro.
accusative.english: I'm looking for a different chair for the office.
accusative.hint: Direct object of suchen, so accusative. Here einen already carries the masculine accusative ending -en, so the adjective drops to the weak ending -en. Compare the nominative above, where the adjective had to do that work.

dative.german: Sie hat es einem anderen Kollegen erzählt.
dative.english: She told it to a different colleague.
dative.hint: Indirect object of erzählen, so dative. Einem shows the masculine dative -em and the adjective takes the weak -en. Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, so it also adds -n outside the nominative singular: Kollegen.

genitive.german: Das ist offensichtlich die Meinung anderer Leute.
genitive.english: That is obviously other people's opinion.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Meinung. There is no article, so the adjective takes the strong genitive plural ending -er. Leute exists only in the plural and adds no genitive ending.

anderer.proTip: The stem is ander- and endings go on top of it: anderer, andere, anderes, anderen, anderem. Written lowercase it is an ordinary adjective (ein anderes Buch) and it stays lowercase in the common noun-like uses too: die anderen (the others), etwas anderes (something else), unter anderem (among other things, abbreviated u. a.).

kaum.note: Adverb meaning 'hardly, barely, scarcely'. Adverbs do not decline for case, and kaum has no endings in any context. It carries its own negative force but does not govern a case, so the examples below demonstrate each case on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing kaum.

nominative.german: Kaum ein Schüler hat die schwere Aufgabe gelöst.
nominative.english: Hardly any student solved the difficult task.
nominative.hint: Subject of hat ... gelöst, so nominative; masculine nominative ein takes no ending. Kaum stands in front of the whole phrase as an invariable adverb and does not change its case.

accusative.german: Ich habe in deinem Text kaum einen Fehler gefunden.
accusative.english: I found hardly a single mistake in your text.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative; einen is the masculine accusative form of ein. Note that in deinem Text is dative, because in describes a location rather than a movement.

dative.german: Er hat kaum mit seinen Eltern gesprochen.
dative.english: He hardly spoke with his parents.
dative.hint: Dative required by the preposition mit, which always governs the dative. Seinen is the dative plural form of sein, and Eltern is a plural-only noun already ending in -n, so no further -n is added.

genitive.german: Kaum die Hälfte des Kuchens war am Abend noch übrig.
genitive.english: Hardly half of the cake was still left in the evening.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after die Hälfte. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Kuchens. Kaum modifies the quantity and stays invariable.

kaum.proTip: Kaum is already negative, so never combine it with nicht — say Ich habe kaum geschlafen, not kaum nicht. Useful combinations: kaum noch (hardly any more), kaum jemand (hardly anyone), and kaum ... da / kaum dass meaning 'no sooner ... than': Kaum war er da, klingelte das Telefon.

im (= in dem).note: A contraction of the preposition in and the dative article dem, meaning 'in the' before masculine or neuter nouns. It is not a word that declines — it is itself already a fixed case form, permanently dative. It cannot be made accusative: in + das contracts to ins instead. The nominative, accusative and genitive below are therefore shown on other phrases in sentences containing im.

nominative.german: Der Schlüssel liegt noch im Auto.
nominative.english: The key is still in the car.
nominative.hint: Subject of liegt, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. The phrase im Auto stays dative because it describes where something is, not where it is going.

accusative.german: Wir haben im Park einen großen Hund gesehen.
accusative.english: We saw a big dog in the park.
accusative.hint: Direct object of sehen, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective großen takes the weak -en after it. Im Park stays dative regardless, because in with a location always takes the dative.

dative.german: Die Kinder spielen den ganzen Nachmittag im Garten.
dative.english: The children play in the garden all afternoon.
dative.hint: Dative, because in is a two-way preposition and here answers wo? (where something is). Im is exactly in + dem, the masculine dative article. Den ganzen Nachmittag is a separate accusative of duration.

genitive.german: Im Büro meines Vaters steht ein alter Schreibtisch.
genitive.english: In my father's office there is an old desk.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Büro. Masculine genitive meines with the noun ending -s: Vaters. The contraction im is unaffected and stays dative.

im (= in dem).proTip: The wo/wohin test decides everything here: in + dative (im, in der) for a static location — Ich bin im Haus; in + accusative (ins, in die) for movement into somewhere — Ich gehe ins Haus. Im is also standard with months and seasons: im Januar, im Sommer.

wenig.note: Means 'little' (with uncountable nouns) or 'few' (as wenige, with plurals). It behaves like an adjective/quantifier and does decline — with one important exception: before an uncountable singular noun it normally stays uninflected (wenig Zeit), while before plurals it takes the regular strong endings (wenige Leute). As a plain adverb (wenig bekannt) it never takes an ending.

nominative.german: Nur wenige Studenten sind gestern gekommen.
nominative.english: Only a few students came yesterday.
nominative.hint: Subject of sind gekommen, so nominative plural. There is no article, so wenig takes the strong nominative plural ending -e. Student is a weak noun, but the nominative plural is Studenten regardless.

accusative.german: Ich habe diese Woche leider sehr wenig Zeit.
accusative.english: Unfortunately I have very little time this week.
accusative.hint: Direct object of habe, so accusative — but nothing in the phrase shows it, because before an uncountable singular noun wenig normally stays uninflected and Zeit is feminine with no accusative ending. The case comes purely from the sentence structure.

dative.german: Er hilft leider nur wenigen Menschen.
dative.english: Unfortunately he only helps a few people.
dative.hint: Dative required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. With no article present, wenig takes the strong dative plural ending -en, and the dative plural noun also ends in -n: Menschen.

genitive.german: Die Meinung weniger Leute zählt hier leider nicht.
genitive.english: The opinion of a few people unfortunately doesn't count here.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Meinung. Without an article, wenig takes the strong genitive plural ending -er. Leute is plural-only and adds no genitive ending.

wenig.proTip: Split it by countability: wenig Geld, wenig Zeit (uncountable, usually no ending) versus wenige Freunde, wenigen Freunden (plural, full endings). Ein wenig means 'a little' and is fixed and invariable. The comparative forms are irregular: wenig – weniger – am wenigsten.

am (= an dem).note: A contraction of the preposition an and the dative article dem, meaning 'at the, on the' before masculine or neuter nouns. It does not decline — it is itself a fixed dative form. An accusative meaning requires the different contraction ans (an + das). The other three cases are therefore demonstrated on separate phrases in sentences containing am.

nominative.german: Am Montag beginnt der neue Kurs.
nominative.english: The new course starts on Monday.
nominative.hint: Subject of beginnt, so nominative — it follows the verb only because the time phrase occupies first position. Masculine nominative der with the weak adjective ending -e on neue.

accusative.german: Wir haben am Wochenende einen guten Film gesehen.
accusative.english: We watched a good film at the weekend.
accusative.hint: Direct object of sehen, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective guten takes the weak -en after it. Am Wochenende remains an unchanging dative time expression.

dative.german: Die Kinder sitzen schon am Tisch.
dative.english: The children are already sitting at the table.
dative.hint: Dative, because the two-way preposition an here answers wo? (position, not movement). Am is precisely an + dem, the masculine dative article.

genitive.german: Am Ende des Tages sind alle ziemlich müde.
genitive.english: At the end of the day everyone is fairly tired.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ende. Masculine genitive des with the noun ending -es: Tages. The contraction am is unaffected and stays dative.

am (= an dem).proTip: Am is the standard form for days and dates — am Freitag, am 3. Mai — and for superlative adverbs: Er läuft am schnellsten. For movement towards a vertical surface use ans: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand, but Das Bild hängt an der Wand.

ganz.note: Two uses. As an attributive adjective it means 'whole, entire' and declines normally (der ganze Tag). As an adverb it means 'quite, completely' and is invariable (ganz gut). The examples below use the attributive adjective so that the declension is visible; the adverb use is covered in the pro-tip.

nominative.german: Die ganze Familie war am Sonntag zu Hause.
nominative.english: The whole family was at home on Sunday.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative. Feminine nominative article die with the weak adjective ending -e on ganze, since the definite article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Er hat den ganzen Tag im Bett geschlafen.
accusative.english: He slept in bed the whole day.
accusative.hint: Accusative — but an accusative of duration, not a direct object, since schlafen takes no object. German puts time spans in the accusative. Masculine den with the weak adjective ending -en.

dative.german: Nach dem ganzen Stress brauche ich dringend Urlaub.
dative.english: After all that stress I urgently need a holiday.
dative.hint: Dative required by the preposition nach, which always governs the dative. Masculine dative article dem with the weak adjective ending -en on ganzen.

genitive.german: Die Bewohner der ganzen Stadt haben mitgefeiert.
genitive.english: The residents of the whole town joined in the celebration.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Bewohner. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; Stadt itself adds no genitive ending, as feminine nouns never do.

ganz.proTip: Attributive ganz declines (die ganze Woche, den ganzen Abend); adverbial ganz does not (ganz gut, ganz schön kalt, ganz allein). Before a place name with no article it also stays uninflected: in ganz Deutschland. Note that ganz gut is a mild 'pretty good', weaker than sehr gut.

zur (= zu der).note: A contraction of the preposition zu and the feminine dative article der, meaning 'to the' before feminine nouns. It does not decline — it is itself a fixed dative form. Zu always governs the dative, even though it expresses movement towards something. The other cases below appear on separate phrases in sentences containing zur.

nominative.german: Der Bus zur Schule fährt jeden Morgen um sieben.
nominative.english: The bus to the school leaves at seven every morning.
nominative.hint: Subject of fährt, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. The attached phrase zur Schule stays dative because zu always requires the dative.

accusative.german: Ich nehme bei gutem Wetter das Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
accusative.english: In good weather I take the bike to work.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehme, so accusative. Neuter das looks identical in nominative and accusative, so the verb is what identifies the case here. Bei gutem Wetter is dative, with the strong adjective ending -em because no article follows bei.

dative.german: Sie geht jeden Tag mit dem Rad zur Uni.
dative.english: She goes to the university by bike every day.
dative.hint: Dative, because zu always governs the dative regardless of the movement it describes. Zur is exactly zu + der, the feminine dative article. Jeden Tag is a separate accusative time expression.

genitive.german: Zur Feier des Geburtstags gab es einen großen Kuchen.
genitive.english: For the birthday celebration there was a big cake.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Feier. Masculine genitive des with the noun ending -s: Geburtstags. Zur itself remains dative.

zur (= zu der).proTip: Remember that zu is a dative preposition even when it clearly means direction — the classic exception to the wo/wohin logic. The forms are zur (zu + der, feminine) and zum (zu + dem, masculine and neuter). Use zu for people and institutions (zum Arzt, zur Schule) and nach for countries and cities without an article (nach Berlin).

selbst.note: Two uses, both invariable. After a noun or pronoun it is an intensifier meaning 'myself, himself, itself' and so on — unlike English, it never changes form for person, number or case. Placed before a phrase it means 'even'. Selbst is not a reflexive pronoun and never takes an ending.

nominative.german: Der Chef selbst hat den Brief unterschrieben.
nominative.english: The boss himself signed the letter.
nominative.hint: Subject of hat ... unterschrieben, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Selbst follows it as an unchanging intensifier and shows no agreement of its own.

accusative.german: Ich habe den Kuchen selbst gebacken.
accusative.english: I baked the cake myself.
accusative.hint: Direct object of backen, so accusative; masculine der becomes den. Selbst here refers back to the subject ich but still takes no ending — English switches between myself/yourself, German does not.

dative.german: Selbst meinem besten Freund habe ich nichts davon gesagt.
dative.english: I didn't tell even my best friend anything about it.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of sagen. Meinem shows the masculine dative -em and the adjective besten takes the weak -en after it. In this position selbst means 'even' and is still invariable.

genitive.german: Die Qualität des Materials selbst ist wirklich gut.
genitive.english: The quality of the material itself is really good.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Qualität. Neuter genitive des with the noun ending -s: Materials. Selbst follows the noun as an intensifier and adds no ending.

selbst.proTip: Position decides the meaning: before a phrase selbst means 'even' (Selbst er weiß das), after it selbst means '-self' (Er selbst weiß das). Selber is a colloquial alternative for the '-self' meaning only, never for 'even'. Don't confuse either with the reflexive pronouns mich, dich, sich.

vom (= von dem).note: A contraction of the preposition von and the dative article dem, meaning 'from the, of the' before masculine or neuter nouns. It does not decline — it is itself a fixed dative form, since von always governs the dative and has no accusative form at all. The other cases appear on separate phrases in sentences containing vom.

nominative.german: Der Brief vom Anwalt kam heute Morgen an.
nominative.english: The letter from the lawyer arrived this morning.
nominative.hint: Subject of kam ... an, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. The phrase vom Anwalt modifies Brief and is dative because von always requires the dative.

accusative.german: Ich habe ein schönes Geschenk vom Chef bekommen.
accusative.english: I got a lovely present from the boss.
accusative.hint: Direct object of bekommen, so accusative. Neuter ein has no ending, so the adjective must show the case with the strong ending -es: schönes. This is mixed declension.

dative.german: Wir sprechen gerade vom neuen Projekt.
dative.english: We're just talking about the new project.
dative.hint: Dative governed by von, contracted with dem. Because dem already marks the case, the adjective neuen takes the weak ending -en. Sprechen von + dative is the fixed pattern for 'to talk about'.

genitive.german: Vom Ergebnis der Prüfung hängt sehr viel ab.
genitive.english: A great deal depends on the result of the exam.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ergebnis. Feminine genitive article der; the noun Prüfung adds no ending, since feminine nouns take no genitive -s.

vom (= von dem).proTip: Von is always dative — there is no von + accusative. The contractions are vom (von + dem) and von der for feminine. In everyday speech von + dative often replaces the genitive: das Auto von meinem Bruder instead of das Auto meines Bruders, though the genitive remains standard in writing.

einmal.note: Adverb meaning 'once, one time'. Adverbs do not decline for case and einmal is invariable in every position. It does not govern a case either, so the four cases below are demonstrated on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing einmal.

nominative.german: Einmal im Jahr besucht uns meine Tante aus Wien.
nominative.english: Once a year my aunt from Vienna visits us.
nominative.hint: Subject of besucht, so nominative — it comes after the verb only because the time expression fills first position. Feminine nominative meine; uns is the accusative object, and im Jahr is dative after in.

accusative.german: Ich habe ihn bisher nur einmal gesehen.
accusative.english: So far I have only seen him once.
accusative.hint: Accusative pronoun, the direct object of sehen — er becomes ihn in the accusative. Einmal is an adverb of frequency and takes no ending.

dative.german: Erzähl mir die Geschichte bitte noch einmal!
dative.english: Please tell me the story one more time!
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of erzählen; die Geschichte is the accusative direct object. Noch einmal means 'once more' and neither part changes form.

genitive.german: Einmal im Monat treffen sich die Mitglieder des Vereins.
genitive.english: Once a month the members of the club meet.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Mitglieder. Masculine genitive des with the noun ending -s: Vereins. Einmal im Monat is a fixed frequency expression and is unaffected.

einmal.proTip: Key combinations: noch einmal (once more), nicht einmal (not even), auf einmal (all of a sudden), and einmal, zweimal, dreimal for counting. In spoken German the shortened mal softens requests and commands: Komm mal her, Warte mal.

beim (= bei dem).note: A contraction of the preposition bei and the dative article dem, meaning 'at the, with, during' before masculine or neuter nouns. It does not decline — it is itself a fixed dative form, since bei always governs the dative and has no accusative form. The other cases below appear on separate phrases in sentences containing beim.

nominative.german: Beim Frühstück klingelte plötzlich das Telefon.
nominative.english: During breakfast the telephone suddenly rang.
nominative.hint: Subject of klingelte, so nominative — it follows the verb because the time phrase occupies first position. Neuter nominative das; beim Frühstück stays dative, as bei always requires the dative.

accusative.german: Beim Aufräumen habe ich meinen alten Ring gefunden.
accusative.english: While tidying up I found my old ring.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative: meinen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective alten takes the weak -en after it. Beim Aufräumen uses a capitalized infinitive as a noun and stays dative.

dative.german: Ich war gestern Nachmittag beim Arzt.
dative.english: I was at the doctor's yesterday afternoon.
dative.hint: Dative governed by bei, which always takes the dative. Beim is exactly bei + dem, the masculine dative article.

genitive.german: Beim Bau des Hauses gab es viele unerwartete Probleme.
genitive.english: During the construction of the house there were many unexpected problems.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Bau. Neuter genitive des with the noun ending -es: Hauses. The contraction beim is unaffected and stays dative.

beim (= bei dem).proTip: Bei is always dative; there is no bei + accusative. Beim plus a capitalized infinitive is the standard way to say 'while doing something': beim Essen, beim Lesen, beim Arbeiten. With people and professions it means 'at someone's place': beim Arzt, beim Friseur, bei meinen Eltern.

meist / meistens.note: Adverb meaning 'mostly, usually'. Both forms are interchangeable in this adverbial sense and neither declines — adverbs have no case forms. The examples below all use meistens, the more common spoken form, and demonstrate the cases on other noun and pronoun phrases. Note that meist- also exists as a declining superlative adjective (die meisten Leute), which is a different use covered in the pro-tip.

nominative.german: Meistens kocht mein Vater am Wochenende.
nominative.english: My father usually cooks at the weekend.
nominative.hint: Subject of kocht, so nominative — it follows the verb only because meistens occupies first position. Masculine nominative mein takes no ending, as ein-words don't in that slot.

accusative.german: Ich nehme meistens den Bus in die Stadt.
accusative.english: I usually take the bus into town.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehme, so accusative; masculine der becomes den. The separate phrase in die Stadt is also accusative, because in expresses movement here rather than location.

dative.german: Er hilft meistens seiner Mutter im Garten.
dative.english: He usually helps his mother in the garden.
dative.hint: Dative required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. Feminine dative seiner; the noun Mutter is unchanged, as feminine nouns are in the singular.

genitive.german: Die Meinung meiner Kollegen ist meistens ähnlich.
genitive.english: The opinion of my colleagues is usually similar.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Meinung; the genitive plural determiner ending is -er, giving meiner. Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, so the plural is Kollegen.

meist / meistens.proTip: As adverbs meist and meistens are interchangeable — meistens is more common in speech. Don't confuse them with the declining superlative of viel: die meisten Leute (most people), den meisten Menschen (to most people). That form takes endings; the adverb never does.

durchs (= durch das).note: A contraction of the preposition durch and the neuter article das, meaning 'through the'. It does not decline — it is itself a fixed case form, permanently accusative, because durch always governs the accusative and never the dative. The nominative, dative and genitive below are therefore shown on other phrases in sentences containing durchs.

nominative.german: Durchs Fenster scheint die warme Sonne.
nominative.english: The warm sun shines through the window.
nominative.hint: Subject of scheint, so nominative. Feminine nominative article die with the weak adjective ending -e on warme, since the definite article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Wir gehen durchs Dorf zum Marktplatz.
accusative.english: We're walking through the village to the market square.
accusative.hint: Accusative required by durch, which governs the accusative in every context. Durchs is exactly durch + das, the neuter accusative article. Note that zum (zu + dem) stays dative, since zu always takes the dative.

dative.german: Durchs Fenster habe ich mit meinem Nachbarn gesprochen.
dative.english: I talked with my neighbour through the window.
dative.hint: Dative required by the preposition mit. Meinem shows the masculine dative -em, and Nachbar is a weak (n-) noun, so it adds -n outside the nominative singular: Nachbarn.

genitive.german: Der Weg durchs Tal des Flusses ist sehr schön.
genitive.english: The path through the valley of the river is very beautiful.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Tal. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -es: Flusses. The contraction durchs is unaffected and stays accusative.

durchs (= durch das).proTip: Durch is one of the always-accusative prepositions — durch, für, gegen, ohne, um. There is no durch + dative, so durchs can never become 'durchem'. Besides physical movement it also expresses means or cause: durch einen Zufall (by coincidence).

quasi.note: Adverb meaning 'practically, virtually, as good as'. It is a Latin loanword and is completely invariable — it takes no endings and does not govern a case, even when it stands directly in front of a noun phrase. The cases below are therefore demonstrated on other phrases in sentences containing quasi.

nominative.german: Der Vertrag ist quasi schon unterschrieben.
nominative.english: The contract is practically signed already.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Quasi modifies the whole predicate and takes no ending of its own.

accusative.german: Sie hat quasi das ganze Projekt allein gemacht.
accusative.english: She practically did the whole project on her own.
accusative.hint: Direct object of machen, so accusative. Neuter das is identical in nominative and accusative, so the verb identifies the case; ganze takes the weak ending -e after the definite article.

dative.german: Er wohnt quasi bei seinen Großeltern.
dative.english: He practically lives at his grandparents' place.
dative.hint: Dative plural required by the preposition bei, which always governs the dative. Seinen shows the dative plural -en, and the noun adds the dative plural -n: Großeltern.

genitive.german: Das ist quasi die Hälfte des Gehalts.
genitive.english: That's practically half of the salary.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after die Hälfte. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Gehalts. Quasi stands outside the phrase and changes nothing.

quasi.proTip: Quasi is fairly informal and always invariable — it never takes an adjective ending even before a noun. Close equivalents are praktisch, so gut wie and sozusagen. In formal writing, so gut wie or nahezu usually reads better.

nach.note: Preposition meaning 'after' (time), 'to' (a destination) or 'according to'. Prepositions do not decline — instead they govern a case, and nach always governs the dative in every one of its meanings, including when it expresses direction. The accusative, nominative and genitive below therefore appear on other phrases in sentences containing nach.

nominative.german: Nach dem Konzert war das Publikum völlig begeistert.
nominative.english: After the concert the audience was completely thrilled.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative — it follows the verb because the time phrase fills first position. Neuter nominative das. Nach dem Konzert is dative, as nach always requires.

accusative.german: Nach der Arbeit trinke ich immer einen starken Kaffee.
accusative.english: After work I always drink a strong coffee.
accusative.hint: Direct object of trinken, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective starken takes the weak -en after it. Nach der Arbeit remains dative.

dative.german: Wir fahren nach dem Frühstück nach Berlin.
dative.english: After breakfast we're driving to Berlin.
dative.hint: Dative governed by nach; neuter dative article dem. The second nach in nach Berlin is the same preposition in its 'to' meaning — city names simply take no article, so no ending is visible there.

genitive.german: Nach der Meinung des Arztes soll ich mich ausruhen.
genitive.english: According to the doctor's opinion I should rest.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Meinung. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -es: Arztes. Nach here means 'according to' and still governs only the dative phrase der Meinung.

nach.proTip: Nach is always dative — never accusative, even though it expresses direction. Use nach for cities and countries without an article (nach Italien, nach Hause), zu for people and institutions (zum Arzt), and in + accusative for countries that take an article (in die Schweiz). In the 'according to' sense it often follows its noun: meiner Meinung nach.

plötzlich.note: Primarily an adverb meaning 'suddenly', in which use it is invariable and takes no ending. The same word also exists as an attributive adjective meaning 'sudden' (ein plötzlicher Regen), and in that use it declines normally. The nominative and genitive below show the declining adjective; the accusative and dative show the invariable adverb with the case carried by other phrases.

nominative.german: Ein plötzlicher Regen hat das Gartenfest unterbrochen.
nominative.english: A sudden shower interrupted the garden party.
nominative.hint: Subject of hat ... unterbrochen, so nominative. This is mixed declension: ein has no ending in the masculine nominative, so the adjective must show the case itself with the strong ending -er.

accusative.german: Plötzlich hörte ich einen lauten Knall.
accusative.english: Suddenly I heard a loud bang.
accusative.hint: Direct object of hören, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective lauten takes the weak -en after it. Here plötzlich is the adverb and has no ending at all.

dative.german: Plötzlich stand er vor meiner Tür.
dative.english: Suddenly he was standing in front of my door.
dative.hint: Dative after the two-way preposition vor, because the sentence describes a position rather than a movement. Meiner is the feminine dative form of mein.

genitive.german: Der Grund des plötzlichen Rücktritts blieb lange unklar.
genitive.english: The reason for the sudden resignation remained unclear for a long time.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Grund. Three separate things happen: the article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun itself adds the genitive -s.

plötzlich.proTip: Adverbial plötzlich never changes (Plötzlich regnete es); attributive plötzlich declines like any adjective (ein plötzlicher Tod, der plötzliche Tod). A common everyday synonym for the adverb is auf einmal.

über.note: Preposition meaning 'over, above' (position) or 'about' (topic). Prepositions do not decline; they govern a case. Über is a two-way preposition: dative for a static position (wo?) and accusative for movement across or over (wohin?). Crucially, in the 'about a topic' meaning it is always accusative, never dative.

nominative.german: Über dem Sofa hängt ein großes Bild.
nominative.english: A large picture hangs above the sofa.
nominative.hint: Subject of hängt, so nominative. Neuter ein has no ending, so the adjective carries the case with the strong ending -es. The phrase über dem Sofa is dative, because it states a position.

accusative.german: Wir haben lange über das neue Problem gesprochen.
accusative.english: We talked about the new problem for a long time.
accusative.hint: Accusative — when über means 'about, concerning', it always takes the accusative regardless of movement. Neuter accusative das with the weak adjective ending -e on neue.

dative.german: Die Lampe hängt genau über dem Tisch.
dative.english: The lamp hangs exactly above the table.
dative.hint: Dative, because über here answers wo? — the lamp is positioned above the table and does not move. Masculine dative article dem.

genitive.german: Über dem Eingang des Museums steht ein altes Zitat.
genitive.english: Above the entrance of the museum there is an old quotation.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Eingang. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Museums. The phrase über dem Eingang is separately dative, marking position.

über.proTip: Three things to keep apart: über + dative for position (über dem Tisch), über + accusative for movement across (über die Straße gehen), and über + accusative for topics (ein Buch über die Geschichte). Über also means 'more than' with numbers: über hundert Euro.

eigentlich.note: Most often a particle/adverb meaning 'actually, in fact', used to reveal the real situation, often contrary to expectation. In that use it is invariable. The same word is also an attributive adjective meaning 'actual, real' (der eigentliche Grund), and there it declines normally. The genitive example below shows the declining adjective; the others show the invariable particle.

nominative.german: Eigentlich ist der Termin schon morgen.
nominative.english: Actually, the appointment is tomorrow already.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. The particle eigentlich sits in first position but takes no ending and does not affect the case.

accusative.german: Eigentlich habe ich heute keine Zeit mehr.
accusative.english: Actually I don't have any more time today.
accusative.hint: Direct object of habe, so accusative. Feminine keine looks the same in nominative and accusative, so the verb identifies the case; Zeit is unchanged, as feminine nouns are in the singular.

dative.german: Eigentlich gehört das Buch meiner Schwester.
dative.english: Actually the book belongs to my sister.
dative.hint: Dative required by the verb gehören, which always takes a dative object. Feminine dative meiner; das Buch is the nominative subject of the sentence.

genitive.german: Der eigentliche Grund seiner Absage ist bis heute unbekannt.
genitive.english: The actual reason for his cancellation is unknown to this day.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Grund; feminine genitive seiner, with no ending on the noun. In this sentence eigentliche is the attributive adjective, taking the weak ending -e after the nominative article der.

eigentlich.proTip: As a particle, eigentlich softens or corrects an assumption: Eigentlich wollte ich nicht kommen. In questions it adds mild curiosity: Was machst du eigentlich beruflich? As an adjective it declines and means 'actual, real'. Distinguish it from wirklich, which asserts truth rather than correcting an expectation.

durch.note: Preposition meaning 'through' (movement from one side to the other) or 'by, by means of'. Prepositions do not decline; they govern a case. Durch always governs the accusative in every meaning — there is no durch + dative. The nominative, dative and genitive below therefore appear on other phrases in sentences containing durch.

nominative.german: Durch das offene Fenster kam frische Luft.
nominative.english: Fresh air came in through the open window.
nominative.hint: Subject of kam, so nominative. There is no article, so the adjective takes the strong feminine nominative ending -e. The phrase durch das offene Fenster is accusative, as durch always requires.

accusative.german: Wir sind gestern durch den dunklen Wald gelaufen.
accusative.english: Yesterday we walked through the dark forest.
accusative.hint: Accusative governed by durch. Masculine accusative den, and because the article already shows the case the adjective dunklen takes the weak ending -en.

dative.german: Durch Zufall habe ich mit meinem alten Lehrer gesprochen.
dative.english: By chance I spoke with my old teacher.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Meinem shows the masculine dative -em and the adjective alten takes the weak -en. Durch Zufall is accusative but has a bare noun, so no ending is visible.

genitive.german: Durch die Hilfe seines Bruders fand er schnell eine Wohnung.
genitive.english: Through his brother's help he quickly found a flat.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Hilfe. Masculine genitive seines with the noun ending -s: Bruders. Die Hilfe itself is accusative after durch.

durch.proTip: Durch belongs to the always-accusative group: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um. Beyond physical movement it marks means or cause (durch harte Arbeit) and the agent in passive sentences when that agent is not a person: Das Haus wurde durch ein Feuer zerstört — compare von for people.

wirklich.note: Adverb meaning 'really', used to stress that something is genuinely true; in that use it is invariable. The same word is also an attributive adjective meaning 'real, actual' (die wirkliche Welt), and there it declines normally. The genitive example shows the declining adjective; the others show the invariable adverb with case carried by other phrases.

nominative.german: Der Film war gestern wirklich spannend.
nominative.english: The film was really exciting yesterday.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Wirklich intensifies the adjective spannend, which is predicative here and therefore takes no ending either.

accusative.german: Er hat wirklich einen guten Job gefunden.
accusative.english: He really has found a good job.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective guten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Das Bild gefällt wirklich allen Gästen.
dative.english: The picture really pleases all the guests.
dative.hint: Dative required by gefallen, which takes a dative object — the thing that pleases is the subject. Allen shows the dative plural -en, and the noun adds the dative plural -n: Gast → Gäste → Gästen.

genitive.german: Der wirkliche Grund seines Erfolgs war harte Arbeit.
genitive.english: The real reason for his success was hard work.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Grund. Masculine genitive seines with the noun ending -s: Erfolgs. Here wirkliche is the attributive adjective with the weak ending -e after the nominative article der.

wirklich.proTip: Adverbial wirklich is invariable (wirklich gut); attributive wirklich declines (die wirkliche Welt, im wirklichen Leben). Keep it apart from eigentlich: wirklich asserts that something is genuinely true, while eigentlich corrects or qualifies an assumption.

gegen.note: Preposition meaning 'against' (opposition or physical contact) and also 'around' with approximate times. Prepositions do not decline; they govern a case. Gegen always governs the accusative — there is no gegen + dative. The other cases below are therefore demonstrated on separate phrases in sentences containing gegen.

nominative.german: Gegen ihn hat kein Spieler eine echte Chance.
nominative.english: No player stands a real chance against him.
nominative.hint: Subject of hat, so nominative; masculine nominative kein takes no ending, like ein. The pronoun ihn after gegen is accusative, because gegen always governs the accusative.

accusative.german: Das Auto ist bei Nebel gegen einen Baum gefahren.
accusative.english: The car drove into a tree in the fog.
accusative.hint: Accusative governed by gegen; einen is the masculine accusative form of ein. Bei Nebel is dative after bei, but the bare noun shows no ending.

dative.german: Gegen den Lärm hilft nur ein Gespräch mit den Nachbarn.
dative.english: Only a conversation with the neighbours helps against the noise.
dative.hint: Dative plural required by mit. The dative plural article is den, and Nachbar is a weak (n-) noun whose plural is Nachbarn. Gegen den Lärm is accusative, not dative, despite looking similar.

genitive.german: Gegen die Entscheidung des Gerichts gab es laute Proteste.
genitive.english: There were loud protests against the court's decision.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Entscheidung. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Gerichts. Die Entscheidung itself is accusative after gegen.

gegen.proTip: Gegen is always accusative — one of durch, für, gegen, ohne, um. Watch the masculine forms, since gegen den Wind and gegen einen Baum are easy to slip into the dative. Gegen also means 'around' for approximate times: Wir kommen gegen acht Uhr.

völlig.note: Means 'completely' as an adverb, in which use it is invariable, and 'complete, total' as an attributive adjective, in which use it declines normally. The examples below use the attributive adjective so that the declension is visible, and several of them deliberately have no article, which forces the strong endings.

nominative.german: Nach dem Sturm herrschte völlige Stille im Dorf.
nominative.english: After the storm complete silence reigned in the village.
nominative.hint: Subject of herrschte, so nominative. There is no article, so the adjective must show the case itself with the strong feminine nominative ending -e.

accusative.german: Ich halte diese Behauptung für einen völligen Unsinn.
accusative.english: I consider this claim complete nonsense.
accusative.hint: Accusative required by für, which always governs the accusative. Einen carries the masculine accusative -en, so the adjective drops to the weak ending -en.

dative.german: Er hat mit völliger Ruhe auf die Frage geantwortet.
dative.english: He answered the question with complete calm.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. With no article present, the adjective carries the case with the strong feminine dative ending -er. Compare the weak -en that would appear in mit der völligen Ruhe.

genitive.german: Das ist ein deutliches Zeichen völliger Erschöpfung.
genitive.english: That is a clear sign of complete exhaustion.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Zeichen. Again there is no article, so the adjective takes the strong feminine genitive ending -er — identical in form to the strong feminine dative, so the sentence position is what distinguishes them.

völlig.proTip: Adverbial völlig never changes (völlig falsch, völlig egal); attributive völlig declines. The trap is the article-less forms, where the adjective has to carry the case itself: völliger Unsinn, mit völliger Ruhe, völliger Erschöpfung. A close synonym is vollständig, and for the adverb also ganz and total.

innerhalb.note: Preposition meaning 'within, inside' — of a space or a period of time. Prepositions do not decline; they govern a case, and innerhalb governs the genitive, not the dative. This makes it one of the most useful everyday genitive prepositions. The nominative, accusative and dative below appear on other phrases in sentences containing innerhalb.

nominative.german: Innerhalb des Gebäudes gilt ein strenges Rauchverbot.
nominative.english: Inside the building a strict smoking ban applies.
nominative.hint: Subject of gilt, so nominative. Neuter ein has no ending, so the adjective takes the strong ending -es. The phrase innerhalb des Gebäudes is genitive, as innerhalb requires.

accusative.german: Innerhalb der Stadt kenne ich wirklich jeden Weg.
accusative.english: Within the city I really know every path.
accusative.hint: Direct object of kennen, so accusative; jeden is the masculine accusative form of jeder and takes der-word endings. Innerhalb der Stadt is genitive feminine, not dative.

dative.german: Innerhalb der Firma spricht man darüber nur mit dem Chef.
dative.english: Within the company people only discuss that with the boss.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Masculine dative article dem. Note the contrast in the same sentence: der Firma after innerhalb is genitive, even though the feminine genitive and dative articles look identical.

genitive.german: Innerhalb einer Woche musst du unbedingt antworten.
genitive.english: You absolutely have to answer within a week.
genitive.hint: Genitive governed by innerhalb; einer is the feminine genitive form of ein. The noun Woche adds no ending, since feminine nouns take no genitive -s.

innerhalb.proTip: Innerhalb takes the genitive: innerhalb des Hauses, innerhalb eines Jahres. When the following noun is a bare plural that would show no genitive ending, German switches to von + dative instead: innerhalb von drei Tagen. Its opposite außerhalb behaves exactly the same way.

komplett.note: Means 'complete' as an attributive adjective, where it declines normally, and 'completely' as an adverb, where it is invariable. The examples below all use the attributive adjective after a definite article, which produces the weak endings throughout; the adverb use is covered in the pro-tip.

nominative.german: Die komplette Ausrüstung liegt schon im Auto.
nominative.english: The complete equipment is already in the car.
nominative.hint: Subject of liegt, so nominative. Feminine nominative article die with the weak adjective ending -e on komplette, since the article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Wir haben den kompletten Text noch einmal gelesen.
accusative.english: We read the complete text through once more.
accusative.hint: Direct object of lesen, so accusative. The article changes from der to den, and the adjective takes the weak masculine accusative ending -en.

dative.german: Mit der kompletten Mannschaft gewinnen wir dieses Spiel sicher.
dative.english: With the complete team we'll definitely win this match.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Feminine dative article der with the weak adjective ending -en. Dieses Spiel is a separate accusative object.

genitive.german: Die Kosten der kompletten Renovierung sind ziemlich hoch.
genitive.english: The costs of the complete renovation are quite high.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Kosten. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun Renovierung adds no genitive ending.

komplett.proTip: Attributive komplett declines (das komplette Menü, den kompletten Tag); adverbial komplett does not (komplett falsch, komplett neu). It is a slightly more informal borrowing — vollständig is the more formal adjective and ganz the more neutral one.

pro.note: Preposition meaning 'per, for each'. It does not decline. Grammatically it governs the accusative, but in practice this is never visible, because pro is always followed by a bare singular noun with no article and no adjective — pro Tag, pro Person. The four cases below are therefore demonstrated on other phrases in sentences containing pro.

nominative.german: Pro Tag kostet das Zimmer achtzig Euro.
nominative.english: Per day the room costs eighty euros.
nominative.hint: Subject of kostet, so nominative — it follows the verb because the pro phrase fills first position. Neuter nominative das. Pro Tag has no article at all, so no case ending is visible on it.

accusative.german: Pro Person rechnen wir einen Liter Wasser.
accusative.english: We count one litre of water per person.
accusative.hint: Direct object of rechnen, so accusative; einen is the masculine accusative form of ein. Pro Person is itself accusative too, but the bare noun Person shows no ending.

dative.german: Pro Monat zahlt sie ihrem Vermieter siebenhundert Euro.
dative.english: Per month she pays her landlord seven hundred euros.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of zahlen; ihrem shows the masculine dative -em. Siebenhundert Euro is the accusative direct object, which is the standard dative-then-accusative pattern.

genitive.german: Pro Kind steigt der Beitrag des Vereins nur leicht.
genitive.english: Per child the club's fee rises only slightly.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Beitrag. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Vereins. Pro Kind remains an article-less phrase with no visible case ending.

pro.proTip: Pro always takes a bare singular noun: pro Tag, pro Stück, pro Kopf, pro Jahr — never 'pro dem Tag' or 'pro einem Tag'. The native alternative je works the same way (je Person). For everyday frequency German often prefers a different pattern altogether: einmal die Woche, zweimal im Monat.

irgendwie.note: Adverb meaning 'somehow, in some way or other'. Adverbs do not decline for case and irgendwie is invariable in every position — it has no endings and does not govern a case. The four cases below are therefore demonstrated on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing irgendwie.

nominative.german: Irgendwie wirkt der neue Kollege heute nervös.
nominative.english: Somehow the new colleague seems nervous today.
nominative.hint: Subject of wirkt, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, but the nominative singular is the one form without the -n.

accusative.german: Wir müssen irgendwie eine bessere Lösung finden.
accusative.english: We have to find a better solution somehow.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative. Feminine eine is identical in nominative and accusative; bessere takes the mixed-declension ending -e after an ein-word in the feminine accusative.

dative.german: Irgendwie muss ich meinem Chef die Wahrheit sagen.
dative.english: Somehow I have to tell my boss the truth.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of sagen; meinem shows the masculine dative -em. Die Wahrheit is the accusative direct object.

genitive.german: Irgendwie hat er den Ton des ganzen Gesprächs verändert.
genitive.english: Somehow he changed the tone of the whole conversation.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ton. The article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s: Gesprächs.

irgendwie.proTip: Irgendwie is invariable, like the rest of the fixed irgend- adverbs: irgendwo (somewhere), irgendwann (sometime), irgendwoher (from somewhere). The one member of the family that does decline is the determiner irgendein: irgendeinen Grund, irgendeiner Frau.

zusammen.note: Adverb meaning 'together, jointly'. Adverbs do not decline for case, and zusammen is invariable. It does not govern a case of its own; when a partner is named, the case comes from the preposition mit, which always takes the dative. The cases below are demonstrated on other phrases in sentences containing zusammen.

nominative.german: Zusammen schaffen die Kinder die Aufgabe ganz leicht.
nominative.english: Together the children manage the task quite easily.
nominative.hint: Subject of schaffen, so nominative plural; the nominative plural article is die for all genders. Die Aufgabe is the accusative object, which looks identical but is identified by the verb.

accusative.german: Wir haben zusammen den ganzen Film gesehen.
accusative.english: We watched the whole film together.
accusative.hint: Direct object of sehen, so accusative. Masculine den with the weak adjective ending -en on ganzen, since the definite article already marks the case.

dative.german: Ich wohne zusammen mit meiner Schwester in Köln.
dative.english: I live together with my sister in Cologne.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit, not by zusammen — zusammen mit is a fixed combination in which mit supplies the case. Meiner is the feminine dative form of mein.

genitive.german: Zusammen bilden diese drei Spieler das Herz des Teams.
genitive.english: Together these three players form the heart of the team.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Herz. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Teams. Zusammen stands outside the phrase and changes nothing.

zusammen.proTip: The fixed pattern is zusammen mit + dative. Watch the spelling: with many verbs zusammen fuses into a separable prefix written as one word — zusammenarbeiten, zusammenkommen, zusammenbrechen — but it stays separate as a plain adverb: Wir essen zusammen.

irgendwann.note: Adverb meaning 'at some point, sometime' — at a time that is not specified. Adverbs do not decline for case; irgendwann is invariable and does not govern a case. The four cases below are therefore demonstrated on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing irgendwann.

nominative.german: Irgendwann kommt bestimmt der richtige Moment.
nominative.english: At some point the right moment will surely come.
nominative.hint: Subject of kommt, so nominative — it follows the verb because irgendwann fills first position. Masculine nominative der with the weak adjective ending -e.

accusative.german: Irgendwann möchte ich einen eigenen Garten haben.
accusative.english: At some point I'd like to have a garden of my own.
accusative.hint: Direct object of haben, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective eigenen takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Irgendwann erzähle ich dir die ganze Geschichte.
dative.english: At some point I'll tell you the whole story.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of erzählen — du becomes dir in the dative. Die ganze Geschichte is the accusative direct object.

genitive.german: Irgendwann während des Sommers besuchen wir euch.
genitive.english: At some point during the summer we'll visit you.
genitive.hint: Genitive required by the preposition während, which governs the genitive. Masculine genitive des with the noun ending -s: Sommers. Irgendwann itself contributes no case.

irgendwann.proTip: Irgendwann is invariable and points to an unspecified time, past or future; irgendwann einmal means 'one day'. Don't confuse it with manchmal (sometimes, repeatedly) or with jemals (ever), which needs a question, a negation or a condition around it.

da.note: Two roles, both invariable. As an adverb it means 'there, here' and points to a place or moment already mentioned. As a subordinating conjunction it means 'since, because' and sends the conjugated verb to the end of its clause. Neither use declines or governs a case, so the cases below appear on other phrases in sentences containing da.

nominative.german: Da hinten wartet dein Freund schon auf dich.
nominative.english: Your friend is already waiting for you back there.
nominative.hint: Subject of wartet, so nominative; masculine nominative dein takes no ending, like ein. Auf dich is accusative, because warten auf always takes the accusative.

accusative.german: Da ich keinen Schlüssel hatte, habe ich geklingelt.
accusative.english: Since I didn't have a key, I rang the bell.
accusative.hint: Direct object of hatte, so accusative; keinen is the masculine accusative form of kein. Here da is the causal conjunction, which is why hatte stands at the end of its clause.

dative.german: Da wir dem Nachbarn geholfen haben, war er sehr dankbar.
dative.english: Since we helped the neighbour, he was very grateful.
dative.hint: Dative required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. Nachbar is a weak (n-) noun, so it adds -n outside the nominative singular: dem Nachbarn.

genitive.german: Da vorne ist das Büro meines Chefs.
genitive.english: My boss's office is right there at the front.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Büro. Masculine genitive meines with the noun ending -s: Chefs. Here da is the locational adverb.

da.proTip: Test which da you have by the word order: as a conjunction it pushes the verb to the end (Da es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause), as an adverb it does not (Da regnet es). Causal da is more formal than weil and normally opens the sentence. Da also fuses into pronominal adverbs: dabei, dadurch, davon, darin.

jemals.note: Adverb meaning 'ever, at any time whatsoever'. It is invariable and does not govern a case. It is also restricted in use: it belongs in questions, negations, conditional clauses and after comparatives, not in plain positive statements. Every example below is built in one of those environments, and the cases are shown on other phrases.

nominative.german: Hat dir jemals ein Lehrer davon erzählt?
nominative.english: Has a teacher ever told you about that?
nominative.hint: Subject of hat ... erzählt, so nominative; masculine nominative ein takes no ending. Dir is the dative object of erzählen. The question form is one of the environments jemals needs.

accusative.german: Ich glaube nicht, dass er jemals ein ganzes Buch gelesen hat.
accusative.english: I don't think he has ever read a whole book.
accusative.hint: Direct object of lesen, so accusative. Neuter ein has no ending, so the adjective carries the case with the strong ending -es. The negation in the main clause licenses jemals here.

dative.german: Hast du jemals deinem Bruder die Wahrheit gesagt?
dative.english: Have you ever told your brother the truth?
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of sagen; deinem shows the masculine dative -em. Die Wahrheit is the accusative direct object.

genitive.german: Wenn du jemals die Unterstützung deiner Familie brauchst, ruf einfach an.
genitive.english: If you ever need your family's support, just call.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Unterstützung; feminine genitive deiner, with no ending on the noun. The conditional wenn-clause is what makes jemals natural here.

jemals.proTip: Jemals needs a question, a negation, a condition or a comparative around it — Hast du das jemals probiert?, schöner als jemals zuvor. In a plain positive statement German uses einmal or schon mal instead: Ich war schon mal in Rom. Its negative counterparts are nie and niemals.

dort.note: Adverb meaning 'there, in that place'. Adverbs do not decline for case, and dort is invariable — it takes no endings and does not govern a case. The four cases below are therefore demonstrated on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing dort.

nominative.german: Dort hinten steht ein altes Haus.
nominative.english: An old house stands there at the back.
nominative.hint: Subject of steht, so nominative — it follows the verb because the adverb fills first position. Neuter ein has no ending, so the adjective carries the case with the strong ending -es.

accusative.german: Dort habe ich meinen ersten Job gefunden.
accusative.english: That's where I found my first job.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative: meinen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective ersten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Dort in dem kleinen Dorf wohnen meine Großeltern.
dative.english: My grandparents live there in the small village.
dative.hint: Dative after in, because the sentence states a location rather than a movement. Neuter dative dem with the weak adjective ending -en. The full form in dem is kept here for emphasis; it would normally contract to im.

genitive.german: Dort beginnt die Grenze des Nationalparks.
genitive.english: That is where the border of the national park begins.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Grenze. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Nationalparks. Die Grenze is the nominative subject.

dort.proTip: Dort is purely locational and slightly more distant or formal than da. Its directional partners are dorthin (to there) and dorther (from there). Da is the more flexible word — it can also mean 'then' and work as a causal conjunction, which dort never does.

bisher.note: Adverb meaning 'so far, up to now'. Adverbs do not decline for case, and bisher is invariable — it takes no endings and does not govern a case. The four cases below are therefore demonstrated on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing bisher.

nominative.german: Bisher ist kein einziger Brief angekommen.
nominative.english: So far not a single letter has arrived.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist ... angekommen, so nominative. Masculine nominative kein takes no ending, like ein, so the adjective must carry the case with the strong ending -er: einziger.

accusative.german: Bisher habe ich nur einen kleinen Fehler entdeckt.
accusative.english: So far I have only discovered one small mistake.
accusative.hint: Direct object of entdecken, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective kleinen takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Bisher hat uns leider niemand geantwortet.
dative.english: So far unfortunately nobody has answered us.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun required by the verb antworten, which takes a dative object rather than an accusative one. Niemand is the nominative subject.

genitive.german: Bisher kennen wir nur die Hälfte der Wahrheit.
genitive.english: So far we only know half of the truth.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after die Hälfte. Feminine genitive article der; the noun Wahrheit adds no ending, as feminine nouns take no genitive -s.

bisher.proTip: Bisher means 'up to this moment' and pairs naturally with the present perfect: Bisher habe ich nichts gehört. Bis jetzt is the everyday equivalent and bislang the more formal one. Don't confuse it with seither (since then), which measures from a past point rather than up to now.
