unten.note: Adverb of place meaning 'below, downstairs, at the bottom'. Adverbs do not decline for case, and unten is invariable. It is not a preposition and never takes a noun after it, so it governs no case at all. The cases below are demonstrated on other phrases in sentences containing unten.

nominative.german: Unten wartet schon der Taxifahrer.
nominative.english: The taxi driver is already waiting downstairs.
nominative.hint: Subject of wartet, so nominative — it follows the verb because the adverb unten fills first position. Masculine nominative article der.

accusative.german: Unten habe ich einen alten Koffer gefunden.
accusative.english: Downstairs I found an old suitcase.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective alten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Unten in der Küche riecht es stark nach Kaffee.
dative.english: Downstairs in the kitchen there is a strong smell of coffee.
dative.hint: Dative after the two-way preposition in, because the sentence states a location rather than a movement. Feminine dative article der. The adverb unten merely adds to the location and takes no ending.

genitive.german: Unten am Ende der Treppe liegt ein alter Teppich.
genitive.english: At the bottom at the end of the stairs there is an old rug.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ende. Feminine genitive article der, with no ending on the noun. The phrase am Ende is itself dative after an.

unten.proTip: Unten states position; nach unten expresses direction ('downwards') and von unten means 'from below'. Keep it apart from the preposition unter, which takes a noun and is two-way (unter dem Tisch / unter den Tisch). Its opposite is oben, with the same pattern: nach oben, von oben.

früher.note: Three related uses. As an adverb it means 'formerly, in the past' and is invariable. It is also the comparative of the adverb/adjective früh ('earlier'). And as an attributive adjective it means 'former' (der frühere Chef), in which use it declines normally. The genitive example below shows the attributive adjective; the others show the invariable adverb.

nominative.german: Früher war das Leben in diesem Dorf viel ruhiger.
nominative.english: In the past life in this village was much quieter.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative — it follows the verb because früher fills first position. Neuter nominative das. In diesem Dorf is dative, marking a location.

accusative.german: Früher hatte mein Großvater einen kleinen Laden.
accusative.english: My grandfather used to have a small shop.
accusative.hint: Direct object of hatte, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective kleinen takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Früher gehörte das Haus meinen Großeltern.
dative.english: The house used to belong to my grandparents.
dative.hint: Dative required by the verb gehören, which always takes a dative object. Meinen shows the dative plural -en and the noun adds the dative plural -n: Großeltern.

genitive.german: Der frühere Direktor der Schule lebt jetzt in Spanien.
genitive.english: The school's former director now lives in Spain.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Direktor; feminine genitive article der, with no ending on the noun. Here frühere is the attributive adjective, taking the weak ending -e after the nominative article der.

früher.proTip: Three uses worth keeping apart: the adverb 'in the past' (Früher war alles besser), the comparative of früh (Ich stehe früher auf als du), and the attributive adjective 'former', which declines (mein früherer Chef, meines früheren Chefs). Only the last one takes endings.

hin.note: Directional particle meaning 'there, to that place' — motion away from the speaker, as opposed to her, which is motion towards the speaker. It is invariable and governs no case. It works as a separable verb prefix (hinlegen, hingehen) and in the postposed pattern zu ... hin. The cases below appear on other phrases in sentences containing hin.

nominative.german: Zum See hin wird der Weg immer schmaler.
nominative.english: Towards the lake the path gets narrower and narrower.
nominative.hint: Subject of wird, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. In the frame zu ... hin, the case comes from zu, which always takes the dative — hence zum (zu + dem) — while hin itself adds only direction.

accusative.german: Leg das schwere Buch bitte dort hin!
accusative.english: Please put the heavy book down over there!
accusative.hint: Direct object of hinlegen, so accusative. Neuter das is identical in nominative and accusative, so the verb identifies the case; schwere takes the weak ending -e after the definite article. Hin is the separable prefix and stands at the end.

dative.german: Ich gehe kurz zu meiner Freundin hin.
dative.english: I'm popping over to my friend's place.
dative.hint: Dative required by zu, which always governs the dative even when it expresses direction. Meiner is the feminine dative form of mein; hin contributes direction but no case.

genitive.german: Zum Ende des Konzerts hin wurde die Musik leiser.
genitive.english: Towards the end of the concert the music got quieter.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ende. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Konzerts. Zum Ende is dative after zu, and hin closes the frame.

hin.proTip: The hin/her pair marks direction relative to the speaker: Geh hin! (away from me) versus Komm her! (towards me). They combine with prepositions — hinein/herein, hinauf/herauf, hinunter/herunter — and hin is a very productive separable prefix: hingehen, hinlegen, hinfahren, hinsetzen. Useful frame: zum Ende hin, zum Abend hin.

schließlich.note: Adverb with two senses: temporal 'finally, in the end', and justifying 'after all', introducing a reason that outweighs the rest. In both uses it is invariable — adverbs take no case endings and govern no case. The cases below appear on other noun phrases in sentences containing schließlich.

nominative.german: Schließlich kam der lang erwartete Brief doch noch.
nominative.english: In the end the long-awaited letter did arrive after all.
nominative.hint: Subject of kam, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e on erwartete. The adverb lang modifies the adjective and takes no ending itself.

accusative.german: Schließlich haben wir doch einen guten Platz gefunden.
accusative.english: In the end we did find a good seat.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective guten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Schließlich hat er seinem Vater die ganze Wahrheit gesagt.
dative.english: In the end he told his father the whole truth.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of sagen; seinem shows the masculine dative -em. Die ganze Wahrheit is the accusative direct object, the usual dative-then-accusative order.

genitive.german: Schließlich war das die Entscheidung des ganzen Teams.
genitive.english: After all, that was the decision of the whole team.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Entscheidung. The article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s: Teams. Here schließlich carries its 'after all' sense.

schließlich.proTip: Two senses, distinguished by context: temporal 'finally' (Schließlich gingen alle nach Hause) and justifying 'after all' (Er muss es wissen, schließlich ist er der Chef). Don't substitute endlich, which adds relief that a wait is over: Endlich bist du da!

ab.note: Preposition meaning 'from, as of' — marking a starting point in time or place. Prepositions do not decline; they govern a case, and ab governs the dative. It is also an extremely common separable verb prefix (abfahren, abholen), where it is simply part of the verb and has no case at all.

nominative.german: Ab morgen gilt der neue Fahrplan.
nominative.english: From tomorrow the new timetable applies.
nominative.hint: Subject of gilt, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Ab morgen has a bare adverb after it, so no case ending is visible there.

accusative.german: Ab nächster Woche brauche ich einen zweiten Schlüssel.
accusative.english: From next week on I'll need a second key.
accusative.hint: Direct object of brauchen, so accusative: einen with the masculine accusative -en and the weak adjective ending -en on zweiten. Note the contrast with nächster Woche, which is dative after ab, with the strong feminine dative ending -er because no article is present.

dative.german: Ab dem ersten Mai wohnen wir in Hamburg.
dative.english: From the first of May we'll be living in Hamburg.
dative.hint: Dative governed by ab. Masculine dative article dem with the weak adjective ending -en on ersten, since the article already marks the case.

genitive.german: Ab dem Beginn des Kurses gibt es keine Pausen mehr.
genitive.english: From the start of the course there are no more breaks.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Beginn. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -es: Kurses. Dem Beginn itself is dative after ab.

ab.proTip: Ab governs the dative: ab dem 1. Januar, ab nächstem Montag, ab einem bestimmten Alter. With bare time words no ending shows at all (ab morgen, ab acht Uhr), which hides the dative. Von ... an means the same thing: von morgen an. Separately, ab is a very productive separable prefix: abfahren, abholen, abnehmen.

vorbei.note: Adverb meaning 'over, past, finished'. It is invariable and does not itself govern a case. When a thing is passed, German uses the fixed frame an + dative + vorbei (an der Kirche vorbei), so the dative there comes from an, not from vorbei. It is also a separable prefix: vorbeikommen, vorbeifahren.

nominative.german: Der lange Winter ist endlich vorbei.
nominative.english: The long winter is finally over.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Vorbei is used predicatively here and takes no ending, as predicative adjectives and adverbs never do.

accusative.german: Ich habe den Bus gerade vorbeifahren sehen.
accusative.english: I just saw the bus drive past.
accusative.hint: Accusative — the object of the perception construction with sehen, which takes an accusative plus a bare infinitive. Masculine der becomes den; vorbei is the separable prefix of vorbeifahren.

dative.german: Wir sind gestern an einem alten Schloss vorbeigefahren.
dative.english: Yesterday we drove past an old castle.
dative.hint: Dative required by an in the fixed frame an ... vorbei — this frame always takes the dative, even though it describes movement. Einem shows the neuter dative -em and the adjective alten takes the weak -en.

genitive.german: Nach dem Ende des Konzerts war der Abend schnell vorbei.
genitive.english: After the end of the concert the evening was quickly over.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ende. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Konzerts. Dem Ende is dative after nach.

vorbei.proTip: Remember the frame an + dative + vorbei: an der Kirche vorbei, an mir vorbei — the dative is the point people most often get wrong, since movement usually suggests the accusative. Predicatively vorbei means 'over': Es ist vorbei. As a prefix it is very common: vorbeikommen (to drop by), vorbeigehen (to go past).

zurück.note: Adverb meaning 'back' — returning to an earlier place or state. It is invariable, takes no endings and governs no case. It is one of the most productive separable verb prefixes in German (zurückgeben, zurückkommen). The cases below are demonstrated on other phrases in sentences containing zurück.

nominative.german: Morgen ist der Chef endlich wieder zurück.
nominative.english: Tomorrow the boss is finally back again.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Zurück is used predicatively here and takes no ending.

accusative.german: Ich habe das geliehene Buch schon zurückgegeben.
accusative.english: I have already given back the borrowed book.
accusative.hint: Direct object of zurückgeben, so accusative. Neuter das is identical in nominative and accusative, so the verb identifies the case; geliehene takes the weak ending -e after the definite article.

dative.german: Er hat seinem Freund das Geld sofort zurückgegeben.
dative.english: He gave his friend the money back immediately.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of zurückgeben; seinem shows the masculine dative -em. Das Geld is the accusative direct object.

genitive.german: Nach der langen Reise ist sie zurück in der Stadt ihrer Kindheit.
genitive.english: After the long journey she is back in the town of her childhood.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Stadt; feminine genitive ihrer, with no ending on the noun. In der Stadt is separately dative, marking a location.

zurück.proTip: Zurück never changes form. As a predicate it means 'back': Ich bin gleich zurück. As a separable prefix it is everywhere — zurückgeben, zurückkommen, zurückrufen, zurückfahren — and in the perfect the prefix stays attached: zurückgekommen. Fixed phrase for tickets: hin und zurück (return).

egal.note: Predicative adjective meaning 'all the same, of no importance'. It is used almost only after sein or werden, never before a noun, and predicative adjectives take no endings in German — so egal is invariable in practice. Its regular pattern is etwas ist jemandem egal: the thing is nominative and the person is dative.

nominative.german: Der genaue Termin ist mir eigentlich egal.
nominative.english: The exact date doesn't really matter to me.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e on genaue. Egal itself stands after the verb as a predicate and takes no ending at all.

accusative.german: Es ist mir egal, welchen Weg wir heute nehmen.
accusative.english: I don't care which way we take today.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehmen in the subordinate clause, so accusative. Welchen is the masculine accusative form of welcher and takes der-word endings.

dative.german: Das Ergebnis war meinem Bruder völlig egal.
dative.english: The result was completely irrelevant to my brother.
dative.hint: Dative marking the person to whom something is egal — this word always pairs with a dative person. Meinem shows the masculine dative -em; das Ergebnis is the nominative subject.

genitive.german: Die Meinung der anderen Gäste war ihr völlig egal.
genitive.english: The opinion of the other guests was completely irrelevant to her.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Meinung. The genitive plural article is der, and the adjective takes the weak ending -en after it: anderen.

egal.proTip: Learn the frame: etwas ist jemandem egal — Das ist mir egal, Es war ihm egal. The person is dative, never accusative. Egal also introduces concessive questions, where it stays uninflected: egal wer, egal was, egal wie teuer. It is not used attributively, so 'ein egaler Termin' is wrong.

sonst.note: Adverb with two senses: 'or else, otherwise', introducing the consequence of not doing something, and 'apart from that, else'. It is invariable and governs no case. Note that in the 'or else' sense it is an adverb, not a subordinating conjunction, so the clause after it keeps normal main-clause word order.

nominative.german: Beeil dich, sonst fährt der Zug ohne uns ab.
nominative.english: Hurry up, or else the train will leave without us.
nominative.hint: Subject of fährt ... ab, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Note that sonst takes first position and the verb stays second — it does not send the verb to the end. Ohne uns is accusative, since ohne always governs the accusative.

accusative.german: Hast du sonst noch einen besonderen Wunsch?
accusative.english: Do you have any other particular wish?
accusative.hint: Direct object of hast, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective besonderen takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Sonst hat mir bei dem Umzug niemand geholfen.
dative.english: Apart from that nobody helped me with the move.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. Bei dem Umzug is also dative, governed by bei. Niemand is the nominative subject.

genitive.german: Sonst ist die Qualität des Materials wirklich ausgezeichnet.
genitive.english: Apart from that the quality of the material is really excellent.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Qualität. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Materials.

sonst.proTip: Two senses to separate: consequential 'or else' (Nimm einen Schirm mit, sonst wirst du nass) and 'else / apart from that' (Sonst noch etwas?, sonst niemand, sonst nichts). Since it is an adverb and not a conjunction, the verb after sonst stays in second position — unlike after weil or damit.

mindestens.note: Adverb meaning 'at least', stating a minimum amount. It is invariable — adverbs take no endings — and it does not govern a case; it simply modifies the quantity that follows, which keeps whatever case its own role in the sentence requires. The cases below are shown on those phrases.

nominative.german: Mindestens zwanzig Leute standen vor der Tür.
nominative.english: At least twenty people were standing in front of the door.
nominative.hint: Subject of standen, so nominative plural. Mindestens modifies the number and takes no ending; Leute is a plural-only noun with no nominative ending. Vor der Tür is dative, marking position.

accusative.german: Für diese Aufgabe brauchst du mindestens einen zweiten Versuch.
accusative.english: For this task you need at least a second attempt.
accusative.hint: Direct object of brauchen, so accusative: einen with the masculine accusative -en and the weak adjective ending -en on zweiten. Für diese Aufgabe is accusative too, since für always governs the accusative.

dative.german: Mindestens meinen Eltern muss ich die Wahrheit sagen.
dative.english: I have to tell at least my parents the truth.
dative.hint: Dative plural indirect object of sagen; meinen shows the dative plural -en and Eltern is a plural-only noun already ending in -n. Die Wahrheit is the accusative direct object.

genitive.german: Mindestens die Hälfte des Geldes ist schon ausgegeben.
genitive.english: At least half of the money has already been spent.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after die Hälfte. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -es: Geldes. Die Hälfte is the nominative subject.

mindestens.proTip: Mindestens states a numerical minimum: mindestens drei Stunden. Wenigstens and zumindest are about concession or consolation instead — Wenigstens hat es nicht geregnet. Related forms: the adjective mindeste (nicht die mindeste Ahnung) and the noun das Mindeste.

je.note: Three distinct uses, all invariable. As an adverb it means 'ever' (in questions and after comparatives). As a distributive preposition it means 'per' and takes a bare noun with no article. And in the correlative je ... desto/umso it introduces a subordinate clause, sending its verb to the end. It never takes an ending.

nominative.german: Je länger der Winter dauert, desto teurer wird das Heizen.
nominative.english: The longer the winter lasts, the more expensive heating becomes.
nominative.hint: Subject of dauert, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. The je-clause is subordinate, which is why dauert stands at the end of it, and the desto-clause then starts with the verb wird.

accusative.german: Hast du je einen schöneren Sonnenuntergang gesehen?
accusative.english: Have you ever seen a more beautiful sunset?
accusative.hint: Direct object of sehen, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the comparative adjective schöneren takes the weak -en after it. Here je means 'ever', which needs a question or comparative around it.

dative.german: Je nach dem Wetter fahren wir mit dem Rad oder mit dem Bus.
dative.english: Depending on the weather we go by bike or by bus.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. The frame je nach also takes the dative, supplied by nach — so dem Wetter is dative as well.

genitive.german: Je Person steigt der Preis des Tickets um zwei Euro.
genitive.english: Per person the price of the ticket rises by two euros.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Preis. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Tickets. Je Person is a bare noun with no article, so no case ending appears there.

je.proTip: Three uses: 'ever' (schöner als je zuvor), 'per' with a bare noun (je Person, je Stück — like pro), and the correlative je ... desto/umso (Je mehr du übst, desto besser wirst du), where the je-clause is subordinate and its verb goes last. Also je nach + dative, meaning 'depending on'.

gerade.note: Two uses. As an adverb it means 'just, right now' and is invariable. As an adjective it means 'straight' (and 'even' of numbers) and declines normally. The genitive example below uses the attributive adjective so the declension is visible; the others use the invariable adverb with the case carried by other phrases.

nominative.german: Gerade jetzt klingelt schon wieder das Telefon.
nominative.english: Right now the telephone is ringing yet again.
nominative.hint: Subject of klingelt, so nominative — it follows the verb because the time phrase fills first position. Neuter nominative das. The adverb gerade takes no ending.

accusative.german: Ich habe gerade einen wichtigen Anruf bekommen.
accusative.english: I have just received an important call.
accusative.hint: Direct object of bekommen, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective wichtigen takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Ich habe gerade mit deiner älteren Schwester telefoniert.
dative.english: I have just been on the phone with your older sister.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Deiner is the feminine dative form of dein, and because the determiner already shows the case the adjective älteren takes the weak ending -en.

genitive.german: Die gerade Linie des Horizonts war deutlich zu sehen.
genitive.english: The straight line of the horizon was clearly visible.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Linie. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Horizonts. In this sentence gerade is the attributive adjective, taking the weak ending -e after the nominative article die.

gerade.proTip: Adverbial gerade is invariable and means 'just now' (Ich esse gerade); adjectival gerade declines and means 'straight' (eine gerade Linie) or 'even' for numbers (gerade Zahlen). Gerade noch means 'only just', and in speech the clipped form grad is very common.

davon.note: Pronominal adverb meaning 'of it, about it, from it'. It is a fusion of da + von and is completely invariable. It already contains the preposition von, so it replaces a whole von-phrase and no separate noun follows it. It refers only to things and ideas, never to people — for a person you say von ihm, von ihr.

nominative.german: Davon hängt der ganze weitere Plan ab.
nominative.english: The whole further plan depends on that.
nominative.hint: Subject of hängt ... ab, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with weak endings -e on both adjectives, since the definite article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Davon habe ich leider nur einen kleinen Teil verstanden.
accusative.english: Unfortunately I only understood a small part of it.
accusative.hint: Direct object of verstehen, so accusative: einen with the masculine accusative -en and the weak adjective ending -en on kleinen.

dative.german: Davon habe ich meinem Chef bisher nichts erzählt.
dative.english: So far I have told my boss nothing about it.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of erzählen; meinem shows the masculine dative -em. Nichts is the accusative object, and davon replaces the von-phrase entirely.

genitive.german: Davon hängt die ganze Zukunft des Projekts ab.
genitive.english: The entire future of the project depends on that.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Zukunft. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Projekts. Die Zukunft is the nominative subject.

davon.proTip: Davon is for things only: Ich habe davon gehört (I heard about it) versus Ich habe von ihm gehört (I heard from him). It belongs to a large family — damit, dafür, danach, dadurch — and an -r- is inserted when the preposition begins with a vowel: darauf, darin, darüber, daran.

direkt.note: Means 'directly, right' as an adverb, in which use it is invariable, and 'direct' as an attributive adjective, in which use it declines normally. The examples below use both: the attributive adjective where the declension is visible, and the adverb where the case is carried by another phrase.

nominative.german: Die direkte Verbindung nach München ist deutlich teurer.
nominative.english: The direct connection to Munich is considerably more expensive.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative. Feminine nominative article die with the weak adjective ending -e on direkte, since the article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Wir nehmen den direkten Weg zum Bahnhof.
accusative.english: We'll take the direct route to the station.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehmen, so accusative. The article changes from der to den and the adjective takes the weak masculine accusative ending -en.

dative.german: Das Hotel liegt direkt neben dem alten Bahnhof.
dative.english: The hotel is right next to the old station.
dative.hint: Dative after the two-way preposition neben, because the sentence states a position. Masculine dative dem with the weak adjective ending -en. Here direkt is the invariable adverb, intensifying the location.

genitive.german: Der Vorteil der direkten Verbindung ist die kurze Fahrzeit.
genitive.english: The advantage of the direct connection is the short travel time.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Vorteil. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun Verbindung adds no genitive ending.

direkt.proTip: Attributive direkt declines (ein direkter Flug, eines direkten Fluges); adverbial direkt does not (direkt vor der Tür, direkt danach). As an adverb before a preposition it sharpens the location to 'right, immediately': direkt am Meer, direkt gegenüber.

dabei.note: Pronominal adverb formed from da + bei, meaning 'in doing so, at the same time' and also 'on one's person'. It is invariable and replaces a whole bei-phrase, so no noun follows it. It refers to things and situations, not people. A third, concessive sense — 'and yet' — is common in speech.

nominative.german: Dabei spielt das Wetter überhaupt keine große Rolle.
nominative.english: The weather plays no big part in this at all.
nominative.hint: Subject of spielt, so nominative; neuter nominative das. Keine große Rolle is the accusative object of the fixed expression eine Rolle spielen.

accusative.german: Ich habe leider keinen Ausweis dabei.
accusative.english: Unfortunately I don't have any ID on me.
accusative.hint: Direct object of haben, so accusative; keinen is the masculine accusative form of kein. Dabei haben is the fixed expression for carrying something with you.

dative.german: Dabei hat mir mein älterer Bruder sehr geholfen.
dative.english: My older brother helped me a lot with that.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. Mein älterer Bruder is the nominative subject, with the strong adjective ending -er because mein has no ending in the masculine nominative.

genitive.german: Dabei geht es um die Zukunft des ganzen Unternehmens.
genitive.english: This concerns the future of the whole company.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Zukunft: the article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s. Die Zukunft is accusative after um, in the fixed expression es geht um.

dabei.proTip: Three senses: 'in the process, while doing that' (Sie las und hörte dabei Musik), 'on one's person' (Hast du Geld dabei?), and concessive 'and yet' (Dabei hatte er es versprochen). It belongs to the da-family: damit, davon, dafür, darauf.

mancher.note: Determiner and pronoun meaning 'some, many a'. It declines fully for case, gender and number and is a der-word: its endings copy those of der/die/das, so an adjective following it normally takes weak endings in the singular. The dictionary form mancher already shows the masculine nominative ending.

nominative.german: Mancher Student unterschätzt die schriftliche Prüfung.
nominative.english: Many a student underestimates the written exam.
nominative.hint: Subject of unterschätzt, so nominative. Masculine nominative mancher mirrors der. Student is a weak (n-) noun, but the nominative singular is the one form without -en.

accusative.german: Manchen Fehler bemerkt man erst viel später.
accusative.english: Some mistakes you only notice much later.
accusative.hint: Direct object of bemerken, so accusative — it stands first for emphasis, with man as the nominative subject. Masculine accusative manchen mirrors den.

dative.german: In manchen Städten ist das Parken völlig kostenlos.
dative.english: In some cities parking is completely free.
dative.hint: Dative plural after in, because the sentence states a location. Manchen shows the dative plural -en, and the noun adds the dative plural -n: Stadt → Städte → Städten.

genitive.german: Die Meinung mancher Kollegen überrascht mich immer wieder.
genitive.english: The opinion of some colleagues surprises me again and again.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Meinung. The genitive plural ending -er mirrors the article der; Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, so the plural is Kollegen.

mancher.proTip: Mancher takes der-word endings, so an adjective after it normally goes weak in the singular: mancher neue Plan, manchen neuen Plan. In everyday German the plural manche is far more common than the singular (manche Leute, manche Tage). There is also an uninflected manch used before ein: manch ein Student.

dadurch.note: Pronominal adverb formed from da + durch, meaning 'thereby, as a result, by that means'. It is invariable and replaces a whole durch-phrase, so no noun follows it and it shows no case itself. It refers only to things, actions and causes, never to people. The cases below appear on other phrases.

nominative.german: Dadurch wurde das ganze Problem noch viel größer.
nominative.english: As a result the whole problem became much bigger still.
nominative.hint: Subject of wurde, so nominative; neuter nominative das with the weak adjective ending -e on ganze. Größer is a predicative comparative and therefore takes no ending.

accusative.german: Dadurch habe ich einen ganzen Arbeitstag verloren.
accusative.english: As a result I lost a whole working day.
accusative.hint: Direct object of verlieren, so accusative: einen with the masculine accusative -en and the weak adjective ending -en on ganzen.

dative.german: Dadurch konnte ich meinem neuen Kollegen endlich helfen.
dative.english: As a result I was finally able to help my new colleague.
dative.hint: Dative required by helfen. Meinem shows the masculine dative -em, the adjective takes the weak -en, and Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, so it adds -n outside the nominative singular.

genitive.german: Dadurch stieg der Wert des Hauses ganz deutlich.
genitive.english: As a result the value of the house rose quite considerably.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Wert. Neuter genitive article des with the noun ending -es: Hauses. Der Wert is the nominative subject.

dadurch.proTip: Dadurch means 'by that means' or 'as a result' and is used only for things. The pattern dadurch, dass introduces the means as a clause: Dadurch, dass er früh aufsteht, schafft er mehr. It belongs to the da-family with damit, davon, dafür and darauf.

solcher.note: Determiner meaning 'such, of that kind'. It declines, but in two different patterns: used on its own it takes der-word endings (solche Leute, solchen Lärm), while after ein it behaves like an ordinary adjective and takes adjective endings (ein solcher Mann). There is also an uninflected form solch used before ein.

nominative.german: Ein solcher Fehler passiert leider sehr leicht.
nominative.english: Such a mistake unfortunately happens very easily.
nominative.hint: Subject of passiert, so nominative. After ein, solcher behaves like an adjective: since ein has no ending in the masculine nominative, solcher must carry the case with the strong ending -er. This is mixed declension.

accusative.german: Solchen Lärm halte ich einfach nicht aus.
accusative.english: I simply can't stand noise like that.
accusative.hint: Direct object of aushalten, so accusative — it stands first for emphasis. With no article present, solcher takes the der-word ending -en, mirroring den.

dative.german: Mit solchen Leuten möchte ich wirklich nicht arbeiten.
dative.english: I really don't want to work with people like that.
dative.hint: Dative plural required by mit. Solchen shows the dative plural -en, and Leute is a plural-only noun that takes the dative plural -n: Leuten.

genitive.german: Die Folgen solcher Entscheidungen sind schwer zu überblicken.
genitive.english: The consequences of such decisions are hard to take in.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Folgen. The genitive plural ending -er mirrors the article der; the noun Entscheidungen is the plural form and adds no further genitive ending.

solcher.proTip: Two patterns to keep apart: alone it is a der-word (solche Leute, solchen Lärm, solcher Entscheidungen), but after ein it is an adjective (ein solcher Mann, einen solchen Mann, einem solchen Mann). The uninflected solch can go before ein: solch ein schöner Tag. In everyday speech so ein usually replaces all of this: so ein Mann.

darin.note: Pronominal adverb formed from da + in with a linking -r-, meaning 'in it, in that'. It is invariable and replaces a whole in-phrase, so no noun follows it and it carries no case of its own. Like the rest of its family it refers only to things, not people — for a person you say in ihm or in ihr.

nominative.german: Darin liegt der eigentliche Unterschied.
nominative.english: Therein lies the real difference.
nominative.hint: Subject of liegt, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e on eigentliche, since the article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Darin habe ich gestern meinen alten Pass gefunden.
accusative.english: I found my old passport in it yesterday.
accusative.hint: Direct object of finden, so accusative: meinen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective alten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Darin unterscheidet er sich deutlich von seinem Bruder.
dative.english: In that respect he differs clearly from his brother.
dative.hint: Dative required by the preposition von, which always governs the dative. Seinem shows the masculine dative -em. Sich unterscheiden von is the fixed pattern.

genitive.german: Darin besteht die eigentliche Stärke seines Arguments.
genitive.english: That is where the real strength of his argument lies.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Stärke. Neuter genitive seines with the noun ending -s: Arguments. Die eigentliche Stärke is the nominative subject.

darin.proTip: The -r- in darin is a linking sound added because in begins with a vowel — the same happens in darauf, daran, darüber, darum. Compare the vowel-less members: damit, davon, dabei. Useful fixed verbs: darin bestehen (to consist in) and sich darin unterscheiden.

beide.note: Determiner and pronoun meaning 'both' — the two together. It exists only in the plural and it does decline. Without an article it takes the strong plural endings (beide, beiden, beider); after a definite article it switches to the weak pattern: die beiden Brüder.

nominative.german: Beide Brüder studieren seit Oktober in Berlin.
nominative.english: Both brothers have been studying in Berlin since October.
nominative.hint: Subject of studieren, so nominative plural. There is no article, so beide carries the case itself with the strong nominative plural ending -e.

accusative.german: Ich habe beide Bücher schon zweimal gelesen.
accusative.english: I have already read both books twice.
accusative.hint: Direct object of lesen, so accusative plural. The strong nominative and accusative plural endings are identical (-e), so the verb is what identifies the case here.

dative.german: Mit beiden Händen hielt er das volle Glas fest.
dative.english: He held the full glass tight with both hands.
dative.hint: Dative plural required by mit. Beiden shows the strong dative plural ending -en, and the noun adds the dative plural -n: Hand → Hände → Händen.

genitive.german: Die Eltern beider Kinder waren sofort einverstanden.
genitive.english: The parents of both children agreed immediately.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Eltern. With no article present, beide takes the strong genitive plural ending -er. The noun Kinder is the plural form and adds nothing further.

beide.proTip: Two patterns: strong endings with no article (beide Freunde, beiden Freunden, beider Freunde) and weak endings after a definite article (die beiden Freunde, den beiden Freunden). Common fixed forms are wir beide, alle beide and das ist beides. For 'both ... and' German uses sowohl ... als auch, not beide.

darauf.note: Pronominal adverb formed from da + r + auf, meaning 'on it' or, in time, 'after that'. The linking -r- appears because auf begins with a vowel. It is invariable, replaces a whole auf-phrase so that no noun follows it, and refers only to things — for a person you say auf ihn or auf sie.

nominative.german: Darauf folgte ein langer und heftiger Streit.
nominative.english: A long and fierce argument followed after that.
nominative.hint: Subject of folgte, so nominative. Masculine ein has no ending, so both adjectives must carry the case with the strong ending -er.

accusative.german: Darauf habe ich einen ganzen Monat gewartet.
accusative.english: I waited a whole month for that.
accusative.hint: Accusative of duration rather than a direct object — German puts spans of time in the accusative. Einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective ganzen takes the weak -en.

dative.german: Darauf hat mir bis heute niemand eine Antwort gegeben.
dative.english: To this day nobody has given me an answer to that.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of geben; eine Antwort is the accusative direct object. Niemand is the nominative subject.

genitive.german: Darauf beruht der Erfolg des ganzen Projekts.
genitive.english: The success of the whole project rests on that.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Erfolg: the article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s.

darauf.proTip: Two senses: spatial 'on it' (der Tisch und die Gläser darauf) and temporal 'after that' (kurz darauf — shortly afterwards). It is the standard partner for verbs governing auf: sich freuen auf → Ich freue mich darauf; warten auf → Ich warte darauf. Its question form is worauf.

darüber.note: Pronominal adverb formed from da + r + über, meaning 'about it' (topic) or 'above it' (position). The linking -r- appears because über begins with a vowel. It is invariable, replaces a whole über-phrase, and refers only to things — for a person you say über ihn or über sie.

nominative.german: Darüber hängt ein großer alter Spiegel.
nominative.english: A large old mirror hangs above it.
nominative.hint: Subject of hängt, so nominative. Masculine ein has no ending, so both adjectives take the strong ending -er to carry the case. This is the spatial sense of darüber.

accusative.german: Darüber habe ich letztes Jahr einen langen Artikel geschrieben.
accusative.english: I wrote a long article about that last year.
accusative.hint: Direct object of schreiben, so accusative: einen with the masculine accusative -en and the weak adjective ending -en on langen. Letztes Jahr is a separate accusative time expression.

dative.german: Darüber habe ich meiner Frau bisher nichts gesagt.
dative.english: So far I have said nothing about that to my wife.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of sagen; meiner is the feminine dative form of mein. Nichts is the accusative object.

genitive.german: Darüber diskutieren die Mitglieder des Vorstands schon seit Wochen.
genitive.english: The members of the board have been discussing that for weeks.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Mitglieder. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Vorstands. Die Mitglieder is the nominative plural subject.

darüber.proTip: Darüber carries both meanings of über: 'about it' with verbs of speaking and thinking (Wir sprechen darüber, Ich denke darüber nach) and 'above it' for position. Also learn darüber hinaus, meaning 'moreover, beyond that'. The question form is worüber.

einzig.note: Adjective meaning 'only, sole, single' — the one and only of its kind. Used attributively it declines normally; used as an adverb (einzig und allein) it takes no ending. The examples below use the attributive adjective, so the endings are visible in all four cases.

nominative.german: Der einzige Zeuge war an diesem Tag leider krank.
nominative.english: The only witness was unfortunately ill that day.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative. Masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Zeuge is a weak (n-) noun, and the nominative singular is its one form without -n.

accusative.german: Sie hat ihren einzigen Sohn nur selten gesehen.
accusative.english: She saw her only son only rarely.
accusative.hint: Direct object of sehen, so accusative. Ihren carries the masculine accusative ending -en, so the adjective drops to the weak ending -en as well.

dative.german: Mit seinem einzigen Freund spricht er über alles.
dative.english: He talks about everything with his only friend.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Seinem shows the masculine dative -em and the adjective takes the weak -en. Über alles is accusative, since über in the 'about' sense always takes the accusative.

genitive.german: Der Name seiner einzigen Tochter ist Anna.
genitive.english: The name of his only daughter is Anna.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Name. Seiner is the feminine genitive form, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun Tochter adds nothing, as feminine nouns take no genitive -s.

einzig.proTip: Attributive einzig declines; the adverb einzig und allein ('solely') does not. Don't mix it up with einzeln (individual, separate) — einzig means there is only one. The negative pattern kein einziger is very common: Es kam kein einziger Gast.

dafür.note: Pronominal adverb formed from da + für, meaning 'for it, for that' and also 'in return, on the other hand'. It is invariable, replaces a whole für-phrase, and refers only to things — for a person you say für ihn or für sie. The cases below appear on other phrases in sentences containing dafür.

nominative.german: Dafür ist der Preis eigentlich viel zu hoch.
nominative.english: For that the price is actually far too high.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. Hoch is predicative here and therefore takes no ending.

accusative.german: Dafür habe ich wirklich einen guten Grund.
accusative.english: I really do have a good reason for that.
accusative.hint: Direct object of haben, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective guten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Dafür danke ich dir ganz herzlich.
dative.english: I thank you most warmly for that.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun required by the verb danken, which takes a dative object rather than an accusative one — du becomes dir.

genitive.german: Dafür brauchen wir unbedingt die Zustimmung des Chefs.
genitive.english: For that we absolutely need the boss's approval.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Zustimmung. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Chefs. Die Zustimmung is the accusative object of brauchen.

dafür.proTip: Dafür is for things only: Ich bin dafür (I'm in favour of it) versus Ich bin für ihn (I'm for him). It also carries a compensating sense: Das Hotel war teuer, dafür aber sehr schön. Standard partner for für-verbs: sich interessieren für → Ich interessiere mich dafür. Question form: wofür.

eigen.note: Adjective meaning 'own' — belonging to someone personally. It declines like any ordinary adjective and is almost always used attributively after a possessive, which puts it into the mixed declension: where the possessive has no ending, eigen has to carry the case itself.

nominative.german: Sein eigenes Zimmer ist leider ziemlich klein.
nominative.english: His own room is unfortunately quite small.
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative. Neuter sein has no ending, so the adjective must show the case with the strong ending -es: eigenes. This is mixed declension.

accusative.german: Ich möchte endlich mein eigenes Auto haben.
accusative.english: I'd finally like to have my own car.
accusative.hint: Direct object of haben, so accusative. Neuter forms are identical in nominative and accusative, so the verb identifies the case; mein again has no ending, so eigenes takes the strong -es.

dative.german: Sie wohnt seit Mai in ihrer eigenen Wohnung.
dative.english: Since May she has been living in her own flat.
dative.hint: Dative after in, because the sentence states a location. Ihrer is the feminine dative form and already shows the case, so the adjective drops to the weak ending -en.

genitive.german: Der Wert der eigenen Arbeit wird oft unterschätzt.
genitive.english: The value of one's own work is often underestimated.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Wert. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun Arbeit adds no genitive ending.

eigen.proTip: Eigen nearly always follows a possessive, which is exactly where mixed declension bites: mein eigenes Haus (strong -es, because mein has no ending) but meinem eigenen Haus (weak -en, because meinem does). Useful fixed phrases: auf eigene Faust, aus eigener Erfahrung, im eigenen Interesse.

wodurch.note: Interrogative and relative pronominal adverb formed from wo + durch, meaning 'by what means' in a question and 'as a result of which' as a connector. It is invariable and refers only to things — for a person you ask durch wen. As a connector it introduces a subordinate clause and sends the verb to the end.

nominative.german: Wodurch entsteht eigentlich dieser seltsame Geruch?
nominative.english: What actually causes this strange smell?
nominative.hint: Subject of entsteht, so nominative. Dieser is a der-word carrying the masculine nominative -er, so the adjective takes the weak ending -e. In a direct question the verb stays in second position.

accusative.german: Wodurch hast du diesen guten Platz bekommen?
accusative.english: How did you get this good seat?
accusative.hint: Direct object of bekommen, so accusative. Diesen shows the masculine accusative -en, mirroring den, and the adjective takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Wodurch konntest du deinem Bruder am Ende helfen?
dative.english: How were you able to help your brother in the end?
dative.hint: Dative required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. Deinem shows the masculine dative -em.

genitive.german: Er kam viel zu spät, wodurch der Beginn des Films verpasst wurde.
genitive.english: He arrived far too late, as a result of which the start of the film was missed.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Beginn; masculine genitive des with the noun ending -s. Here wodurch is a connector, which is why the verb phrase verpasst wurde stands at the end of its clause.

wodurch.proTip: Wodurch is the question-and-relative partner of dadurch, and like it refers only to things; for people use durch wen. The whole family works this way: womit/damit, wofür/dafür, worauf/darauf. A linking -r- appears before a vowel: worauf, worin, worüber.

gesamt.note: Adjective meaning 'entire, total, whole'. It declines like any ordinary adjective and is used attributively before a noun, normally with an article, which means the weak endings are the ones you meet most often. It is not used as an adverb, unlike ganz.

nominative.german: Die gesamte Familie kam zu der kleinen Feier.
nominative.english: The entire family came to the small celebration.
nominative.hint: Subject of kam, so nominative. Feminine nominative article die with the weak adjective ending -e, since the definite article already marks the case.

accusative.german: Er hat den gesamten Betrag sofort in bar bezahlt.
accusative.english: He paid the entire amount immediately in cash.
accusative.hint: Direct object of bezahlen, so accusative. The article changes from der to den and the adjective takes the weak masculine accusative ending -en.

dative.german: Mit dem gesamten Team fahren wir im Mai nach Wien.
dative.english: In May we're travelling to Vienna with the entire team.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Neuter dative article dem with the weak adjective ending -en on gesamten.

genitive.german: Die Kosten der gesamten Renovierung waren am Ende enorm.
genitive.english: The costs of the entire renovation were enormous in the end.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Kosten. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun adds no genitive ending.

gesamt.proTip: Gesamt is a shade more formal than ganz and, unlike ganz, does not work as an adverb — you can say ganz gut but not 'gesamt gut'. It is very productive in compounds: die Gesamtkosten, das Gesamtergebnis, die Gesamtzahl.

sondern.note: Coordinating conjunction meaning 'but rather', used to replace something just rejected. It is invariable and governs no case of its own; as a coordinating conjunction it does not change word order either. The phrase after sondern simply takes the same case as the element it corrects — which is what the examples below demonstrate.

nominative.german: Nicht mein Bruder, sondern meine Schwester hat angerufen.
nominative.english: Not my brother but my sister called.
nominative.hint: Nominative, because it replaces mein Bruder as the subject of hat angerufen. Sondern passes the case through rather than assigning one.

accusative.german: Ich möchte heute nicht den Kaffee, sondern den Tee.
accusative.english: Today I would like not the coffee but the tea.
accusative.hint: Accusative, because it replaces den Kaffee as the direct object of möchte. Masculine der becomes den in both halves — the case is copied, not newly assigned.

dative.german: Ich habe es nicht meinem Chef, sondern meinem Kollegen erzählt.
dative.english: I told it not to my boss but to my colleague.
dative.hint: Dative, because it replaces meinem Chef as the indirect object of erzählen. Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, so it adds -n outside the nominative singular.

genitive.german: Das ist nicht das Auto meines Vaters, sondern das meiner Mutter.
genitive.english: That is not my father's car but my mother's.
genitive.hint: Genitive, because it replaces meines Vaters in the same possessive role. Meiner is the feminine genitive form, and the noun Mutter adds no genitive ending.

sondern.proTip: Sondern always needs a negation in front of it (nicht ... sondern, kein ... sondern). Where there is no correction, use aber: Er ist klein, aber sehr stark. Note the very common frame nicht nur ... sondern auch, and remember that as a coordinating conjunction sondern never sends the verb to the end.

letzt.note: Adjective meaning 'last, final, most recent'. It declines like any ordinary adjective and is never used in its bare dictionary form — it always carries an ending. Because it nearly always follows a definite article or a preposition with one, the weak endings are the ones you meet most often.

nominative.german: Der letzte Zug fährt schon um Mitternacht.
nominative.english: The last train leaves as early as midnight.
nominative.hint: Subject of fährt, so nominative. Masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e, since the article already shows the case.

accusative.german: Ich habe gestern zum Glück den letzten Platz bekommen.
accusative.english: Luckily I got the last seat yesterday.
accusative.hint: Direct object of bekommen, so accusative. The article changes from der to den and the adjective takes the weak masculine accusative ending -en.

dative.german: In der letzten Woche war ich ziemlich krank.
dative.english: Last week I was quite ill.
dative.hint: Dative after in, which takes the dative for periods of time. Feminine dative article der with the weak adjective ending -en.

genitive.german: Das Ergebnis der letzten Prüfung war überraschend gut.
genitive.english: The result of the last exam was surprisingly good.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Ergebnis. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun Prüfung adds no genitive ending.

letzt.proTip: Letzt- never appears without an ending: der letzte Tag, ein letzter Versuch, letzten Endes. Time expressions come in two shapes, both correct: letzte Woche and in der letzten Woche. Keep it apart from the adverb zuletzt ('last, most recently') and from letztendlich ('in the end').

weshalb.note: Adverb used in two ways: as an interrogative meaning 'why', and as a connector meaning 'which is why'. It is invariable and governs no case. The word order differs between the two: in a direct question the verb stays in second position, while as a connector it introduces a subordinate clause with the verb at the end.

nominative.german: Weshalb ist der neue Plan eigentlich besser?
nominative.english: Why is the new plan actually better?
nominative.hint: Subject of ist, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. This is a direct question, so the verb ist stands in second position.

accusative.german: Ich habe den Zug verpasst, weshalb ich einen anderen Weg nehmen musste.
accusative.english: I missed the train, which is why I had to take a different route.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehmen, so accusative: einen with the masculine accusative -en and the weak adjective ending -en. Here weshalb is a connector, which is why musste stands at the end of its clause.

dative.german: Weshalb hast du deinem Bruder gestern nicht geantwortet?
dative.english: Why didn't you answer your brother yesterday?
dative.hint: Dative required by antworten, which takes a dative object rather than an accusative one. Deinem shows the masculine dative -em.

genitive.german: Er war lange krank, weshalb der Beginn des Kurses verschoben wurde.
genitive.english: He was ill for a long time, which is why the start of the course was postponed.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Beginn. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -es: Kurses. The connector weshalb again sends the verb phrase to the end.

weshalb.proTip: As a question word weshalb is a slightly more formal alternative to warum, and weswegen and wieso are close relatives. As a connector it is extremely useful for joining a cause to its consequence: Es regnete, weshalb wir zu Hause blieben. Watch the word order switch between the two uses.

nahe / näher.note: Adjective and adverb meaning 'near', with the comparative näher ('nearer') and the superlative am nächsten. Used attributively it declines like any adjective. It can also work as a preposition, and in that use it governs the dative. Both the base form and the comparative are shown below.

nominative.german: Der nahe Wald beginnt gleich hinter dem Haus.
nominative.english: The nearby forest begins right behind the house.
nominative.hint: Subject of beginnt, so nominative. Masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Hinter dem Haus is dative, marking a position.

accusative.german: Wir haben gestern den näheren Weg genommen.
accusative.english: Yesterday we took the nearer route.
accusative.hint: Direct object of nehmen, so accusative. The comparative stem näher- takes the weak masculine accusative ending -en after the article den.

dative.german: Das Hotel liegt nahe dem alten Hafen.
dative.english: The hotel is situated near the old harbour.
dative.hint: Dative governed by nahe used as a preposition — this is one of the dative prepositions. Masculine dative article dem with the weak adjective ending -en on alten.

genitive.german: Er kennt die Namen der näheren Verwandten nicht mehr.
genitive.english: He no longer knows the names of the closer relatives.
genitive.hint: Genitive plural expressing 'of' after Namen. The genitive plural article is der and the adjective takes the weak ending -en. Verwandten is an adjectival noun and takes adjective endings too.

nahe / näher.proTip: Forms to remember: nah/nahe – näher – am nächsten, with an umlaut in the comparative. As a preposition nahe takes the dative (nahe dem Fluss), but in everyday German in der Nähe von is far more common. The derived nächst- means 'next' or 'nearest': die nächste Woche, der nächste Bahnhof.

umso.note: Particle meaning 'all the more', always followed by a comparative. It is invariable and governs no case. Its main home is the correlative je ... umso, where the je-clause is subordinate (verb at the end) and the umso-clause follows with umso + comparative and then the verb. Desto is fully interchangeable with it.

nominative.german: Je länger man wartet, umso größer wird das Problem.
nominative.english: The longer you wait, the bigger the problem gets.
nominative.hint: Subject of wird, so nominative; neuter nominative das. Größer is a predicative comparative and therefore takes no ending. Note that wartet stands at the end of the je-clause, because that clause is subordinate.

accusative.german: Das Wetter war schlecht, umso mehr haben wir den warmen Tee genossen.
accusative.english: The weather was bad, so all the more did we enjoy the warm tea.
accusative.hint: Direct object of genießen, so accusative. Masculine der becomes den and the adjective warmen takes the weak ending -en after it.

dative.german: Je älter er wird, umso ähnlicher wird er seinem Vater.
dative.english: The older he gets, the more he resembles his father.
dative.hint: Dative required by the adjective ähnlich, which takes a dative complement — jemandem ähnlich sein. Seinem shows the masculine dative -em.

genitive.german: Umso wichtiger wird dadurch die Rolle des ganzen Teams.
genitive.english: The role of the whole team thereby becomes all the more important.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Rolle: the article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s.

umso.proTip: Umso must be followed by a comparative — umso besser, umso schwieriger, umso mehr. In je ... umso it is completely interchangeable with desto. On its own it reacts to what was just said: Umso besser! (All the better!). Watch the word order: the je-clause puts its verb last, the umso-clause does not.

lange.note: Adverb meaning 'for a long time'. In this adverbial use it is invariable and governs no case. It is related to the adjective lang, which does decline (ein langer Weg) — the -e here is not a case ending but simply part of the adverb form. The cases below appear on other phrases in sentences containing lange.

nominative.german: Lange war der alte Weg zum See gesperrt.
nominative.english: For a long time the old path to the lake was closed.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative — it follows the verb because lange fills first position. Masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e.

accusative.german: Wir haben lange einen guten Platz gesucht.
accusative.english: We looked for a good spot for a long time.
accusative.hint: Direct object of suchen, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective guten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Lange hat mir niemand die ganze Wahrheit gesagt.
dative.english: For a long time nobody told me the whole truth.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of sagen; die ganze Wahrheit is the accusative direct object and niemand the nominative subject.

genitive.german: Lange war das die offizielle Politik der ganzen Regierung.
genitive.english: For a long time that was the official policy of the entire government.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Politik. Feminine genitive article der with the weak adjective ending -en; the noun adds no genitive ending.

lange.proTip: Lange is the adverb and never changes; lang is the adjective and declines (ein langer Tag, einen langen Tag). Comparative länger, superlative am längsten. Useful combinations: schon lange (for a long time now), nicht lange (not for long) and lange nicht, which means 'not by a long way'.

gar.note: Particle used to strengthen a negation — 'at all'. It is invariable, takes no endings and governs no case; it simply intensifies nicht, kein or nichts. The cases below are therefore demonstrated on other noun and pronoun phrases in sentences containing gar. A separate adjective gar, meaning 'cooked through', is noted in the pro-tip.

nominative.german: Gar kein Mensch war um diese Zeit auf der Straße.
nominative.english: Not a single person was on the street at that time.
nominative.hint: Subject of war, so nominative; masculine nominative kein takes no ending, like ein. Mensch is a weak (n-) noun, and the nominative singular is its one form without -en.

accusative.german: Er hat gar keinen Versuch gemacht, sich zu entschuldigen.
accusative.english: He made no attempt at all to apologise.
accusative.hint: Direct object of machen, so accusative; keinen is the masculine accusative form of kein. Gar merely strengthens the negation and takes no ending.

dative.german: Das neue Lied hat mir gar nicht gefallen.
dative.english: I didn't like the new song at all.
dative.hint: Dative pronoun required by gefallen, which takes a dative object — the thing that pleases is the nominative subject, here das neue Lied.

genitive.german: Von dem Plan des Chefs hielt sie überhaupt gar nichts.
genitive.english: She thought nothing at all of the boss's plan.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Plan. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Chefs. Dem Plan is dative after von, in the fixed expression halten von.

gar.proTip: Gar lives almost entirely in negations: gar nicht, gar kein, gar nichts, gar niemand. It is close in force to überhaupt and the two often combine (überhaupt gar nichts). Two separate words worth keeping apart: the cooking adjective gar (Die Kartoffeln sind gar) and sogar, which means 'even'.

alleine.note: Adverb meaning 'alone, on one's own'. It is a variant of allein, slightly more colloquial, and the two are interchangeable in this sense. As an adverb it is invariable — it takes no endings and governs no case. The cases below are demonstrated on other phrases in sentences containing alleine.

nominative.german: Alleine schafft der Junge diese Aufgabe nicht.
nominative.english: The boy can't manage this task on his own.
nominative.hint: Subject of schafft, so nominative — it follows the verb because alleine fills first position. Junge is a weak (n-) noun, and the nominative singular is its one form without -n.

accusative.german: Sie hat den ganzen Kuchen alleine gegessen.
accusative.english: She ate the whole cake by herself.
accusative.hint: Direct object of essen, so accusative. Masculine der becomes den and the adjective ganzen takes the weak ending -en after it.

dative.german: Alleine hilft er seiner alten Nachbarin jeden Tag.
dative.english: On his own he helps his old neighbour every day.
dative.hint: Dative required by helfen, which always takes a dative object. Seiner is the feminine dative form and the adjective takes the weak ending -en. Jeden Tag is a separate accusative time expression.

genitive.german: Alleine war sie mit der Pflege des kranken Vaters überfordert.
genitive.english: On her own she was overwhelmed by the care of her sick father.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Pflege: the article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s. Der Pflege is dative after mit.

alleine.proTip: Alleine and allein mean the same thing; alleine is the more colloquial form and both are invariable as adverbs. Allein has two further senses worth knowing: 'merely, just' (Allein der Gedanke macht mich nervös) and, in literary German, 'however'. Ganz allein adds emphasis.

sogar.note: Adverb meaning 'even', used to emphasise something unexpected. It is invariable — adverbs take no case endings — and it governs no case; it simply stands in front of the element it highlights, which keeps whatever case its own role requires. The cases below are shown on those phrases.

nominative.german: Sogar der strenge Direktor hat am Ende applaudiert.
nominative.english: Even the strict director applauded in the end.
nominative.hint: Subject of hat ... applaudiert, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Sogar highlights the phrase but does not change its case.

accusative.german: Er hat sogar seinen alten Wagen verkauft.
accusative.english: He even sold his old car.
accusative.hint: Direct object of verkaufen, so accusative: seinen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective alten takes the weak -en after it.

dative.german: Sogar den kleinen Kindern hat der Film gut gefallen.
dative.english: Even the small children liked the film.
dative.hint: Dative plural required by gefallen. The dative plural article is den, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the dative plural -n: Kindern.

genitive.german: Sogar die Mitglieder des Vorstands waren völlig überrascht.
genitive.english: Even the members of the board were completely surprised.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Mitglieder. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Vorstands.

sogar.proTip: Sogar normally stands directly before the element it emphasises, and it is invariable. Selbst placed before a phrase means the same thing (Selbst der Chef kam), but selbst after a noun means '-self' — that is the distinction to watch. The negative counterpart is nicht einmal: Nicht einmal der Chef kam.

bewusst.note: Adjective meaning 'conscious, aware' or 'deliberate'. Used attributively it declines normally; used predicatively (as in Ich bin mir dessen bewusst) it takes no ending, as all predicative adjectives in German. It also heads one of the most useful genitive constructions in the language: sich einer Sache bewusst sein.

nominative.german: Eine bewusste Entscheidung braucht immer etwas Zeit.
nominative.english: A deliberate decision always takes a little time.
nominative.hint: Subject of braucht, so nominative. Feminine eine is identical in nominative and accusative; the adjective takes the mixed-declension ending -e after an ein-word in the feminine nominative.

accusative.german: Er hat dabei einen ganz bewussten Fehler gemacht.
accusative.english: In doing so he made a quite deliberate mistake.
accusative.hint: Direct object of machen, so accusative: einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective takes the weak -en. The adverb ganz modifies the adjective and takes no ending itself.

dative.german: Mit bewusster Ruhe hat sie auf die Vorwürfe geantwortet.
dative.english: She answered the accusations with deliberate calm.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. With no article present, the adjective must carry the case itself with the strong feminine dative ending -er.

genitive.german: Ich bin mir des Risikos durchaus bewusst.
genitive.english: I am quite aware of the risk.
genitive.hint: Genitive governed by the construction sich einer Sache bewusst sein, which takes a genitive complement. Neuter genitive des with the noun ending -s. Mir is a separate dative reflexive pronoun, and bewusst is predicative here, so it takes no ending.

bewusst.proTip: Learn the frame sich (dative) + genitive + bewusst sein: Ich bin mir der Gefahr bewusst, Er war sich seines Fehlers bewusst. It is one of the few genitive constructions still fully alive in everyday German. The adverb bewusst means 'deliberately' (Das habe ich bewusst getan), and the noun is das Bewusstsein.

lassen.note: Verb meaning 'to let, to allow', 'to have something done', and 'to leave behind'. Verbs do not decline for case — they conjugate (ich lasse, er lässt, er ließ). What lassen does is assign case: its subject is nominative and its object is accusative, and it very often carries a second infinitive. The cases below are shown on the noun phrases around it.

nominative.german: Der Lehrer lässt die Schüler heute etwas früher gehen.
nominative.english: The teacher is letting the students leave a little earlier today.
nominative.hint: Subject of lässt, so nominative — lassen has no case form itself but requires a nominative subject. Note the vowel change in the present tense: lassen becomes lässt in the third person singular.

accusative.german: Ich lasse mein Auto morgen endlich reparieren.
accusative.english: Tomorrow I'm finally having my car repaired.
accusative.hint: Accusative object of lassen. Neuter mein has no ending and is identical in nominative and accusative, so the verb identifies the case. This is the 'have something done' use, with the infinitive reparieren.

dative.german: Lass mir bitte noch ein Stück Kuchen übrig!
dative.english: Please leave me a piece of cake!
dative.hint: Dative indirect object — the person for whom something is left. Ein Stück Kuchen is the accusative direct object of übrig lassen. Lass is the du-imperative, formed without an ending.

genitive.german: Der Chef lässt die Unterlagen des neuen Kunden sofort prüfen.
genitive.english: The boss is having the new client's documents checked immediately.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Unterlagen: the article becomes des and the adjective takes the weak ending -en. Kunde is a weak (n-) noun, so its genitive singular is Kunden, not 'Kundes'.

lassen.proTip: Lassen is strong: lassen – ließ – hat gelassen. But with a second infinitive the perfect takes a double infinitive instead: Ich habe das Auto reparieren lassen, never 'gelassen'. Three core senses: allow (Lass mich gehen), have something done (Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden), and leave behind (Ich habe den Schlüssel zu Hause gelassen). Sich lassen + infinitive expresses possibility: Das lässt sich machen.

stecken.note: Verb meaning 'to put/stick something into' when transitive, and 'to be stuck, to be inside' when intransitive. Verbs do not decline for case; they conjugate and assign case. Stecken shows this neatly: used transitively it takes an accusative object plus a direction, and used intransitively it takes a dative location.

nominative.german: Der Schlüssel steckt noch im Schloss.
nominative.english: The key is still in the lock.
nominative.hint: Subject of steckt, so nominative; masculine nominative article der. This is the intransitive use, where the thing stuck is the subject and the place is dative: im Schloss.

accusative.german: Er steckte den Brief schnell in die Tasche.
accusative.english: He quickly put the letter into his pocket.
accusative.hint: Direct object of the transitive stecken, so accusative; masculine der becomes den. Note that in die Tasche is accusative too, but for a different reason — in takes the accusative for movement into somewhere.

dative.german: Das Auto steckte stundenlang im tiefen Schnee.
dative.english: The car was stuck in deep snow for hours.
dative.hint: Dative after in, because the intransitive stecken describes a position rather than a movement. Im is in + dem, and the adjective takes the weak ending -en after it.

genitive.german: In der Tasche des alten Mantels steckte ein kleiner Zettel.
genitive.english: A small note was stuck in the pocket of the old coat.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Tasche: the article becomes des, the adjective takes the weak ending -en, and the noun adds the genitive -s. In der Tasche is itself dative, marking position.

stecken.proTip: The pair to learn is transitive stecken (accusative object + direction: etwas in die Tasche stecken) versus intransitive stecken (dative location: im Schloss stecken). In modern German it is weak — steckte, hat gesteckt — though the old strong past stak still turns up in writing. Also stecken bleiben, to get stuck.

wollen.note: Modal verb meaning 'to want'. Verbs do not decline for case — wollen conjugates irregularly (ich will, du willst, er will) and its job here is to assign case: a nominative subject, and an accusative object on the main verb it accompanies. The cases below are shown on the noun and pronoun phrases around it.

nominative.german: Mein kleiner Bruder will unbedingt mitkommen.
nominative.english: My little brother really wants to come along.
nominative.hint: Subject of will, so nominative. Masculine mein has no ending, so the adjective must carry the case with the strong ending -er: kleiner. This is mixed declension.

accusative.german: Ich will mir bald einen neuen Computer kaufen.
accusative.english: I want to buy myself a new computer soon.
accusative.hint: Direct object of kaufen, so accusative: einen shows the masculine accusative -en and the adjective neuen takes the weak -en. Mir is a dative reflexive pronoun, marking who benefits.

dative.german: Sie will ihrer Mutter eine große Freude machen.
dative.english: She wants to give her mother a great deal of pleasure.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object in the fixed expression jemandem eine Freude machen. Ihrer is the feminine dative form; eine große Freude is the accusative direct object.

genitive.german: Er will die Unterstützung seiner Familie nicht verlieren.
genitive.english: He doesn't want to lose his family's support.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Unterstützung; seiner is the feminine genitive form and the noun adds no ending. Die Unterstützung is the accusative object of verlieren.

wollen.proTip: Like all modals, wollen has no -t in the third person singular: er will, not 'er willt'. Past: wollte. The classic false friend — will means 'wants', not the English future 'will'; German builds the future with werden. With a second verb the perfect takes a double infinitive: Ich habe gehen wollen.

spezialisieren.note: Verb meaning 'to specialise', used reflexively: sich spezialisieren auf + accusative. Verbs do not decline for case. What matters here is the government: the reflexive pronoun is accusative (mich, dich, sich), and the field of specialisation is introduced by auf, which in this fixed pattern always takes the accusative.

nominative.german: Der junge Arzt spezialisiert sich auf Kinderheilkunde.
nominative.english: The young doctor is specialising in paediatrics.
nominative.hint: Subject of spezialisiert, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Sich is the accusative reflexive pronoun belonging to the verb.

accusative.german: Die Firma hat sich auf einen sehr kleinen Markt spezialisiert.
accusative.english: The company has specialised in a very small market.
accusative.hint: Accusative required by auf in the fixed pattern sich spezialisieren auf — this auf is always accusative, never dative, even though nothing moves. Einen carries the masculine accusative -en and the adjective takes the weak -en.

dative.german: Zusammen mit ihrem Kollegen hat sie sich auf Steuerrecht spezialisiert.
dative.english: Together with her colleague she has specialised in tax law.
dative.hint: Dative required by mit. Ihrem shows the masculine dative -em, and Kollege is a weak (n-) noun, so it adds -n outside the nominative singular.

genitive.german: Die Arbeit des spezialisierten Teams ist sehr gefragt.
genitive.english: The work of the specialised team is much in demand.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing 'of' after Arbeit. Here spezialisiert is the past participle used as an attributive adjective, so it declines like one — weak -en after the genitive article des, with the noun adding -s.

spezialisieren.proTip: Always reflexive in this meaning, and always with auf + accusative: Ich spezialisiere mich auf moderne Literatur. The reflexive pronoun is accusative, so mich and dich, not mir and dir. The participle spezialisiert doubles as an adjective and then takes endings. Related noun: die Spezialisierung.

sollen.note: Modal verb meaning 'should, to be supposed to' — an obligation or expectation coming from someone else. Verbs do not decline for case; sollen conjugates irregularly (ich soll, du sollst, er soll) and assigns a nominative subject, while the accusative object belongs to the main verb it accompanies.

nominative.german: Der neue Mitarbeiter soll morgen früh anfangen.
nominative.english: The new employee is supposed to start tomorrow morning.
nominative.hint: Subject of soll, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. Note the missing -t in the third person singular, which is typical of modal verbs.

accusative.german: Du sollst den Arzt sofort anrufen.
accusative.english: You're supposed to call the doctor immediately.
accusative.hint: Direct object of anrufen, so accusative; masculine der becomes den. Anrufen takes a plain accusative object in German, unlike English 'to call to someone'.

dative.german: Ich soll dir schöne Grüße von deiner Tante bestellen.
dative.english: I'm to pass on warm greetings to you from your aunt.
dative.hint: Dative indirect object of bestellen — du becomes dir. Schöne Grüße is the accusative direct object, and von deiner Tante is dative after von.

genitive.german: Wir sollen die Anweisungen des Chefs ganz genau befolgen.
genitive.english: We are supposed to follow the boss's instructions very precisely.
genitive.hint: Genitive expressing possession after Anweisungen. Masculine genitive article des with the noun ending -s: Chefs. Die Anweisungen is the accusative object of befolgen.

sollen.proTip: Sollen marks an expectation imposed from outside, weaker than müssen: Ich soll um acht da sein. It also reports hearsay — Er soll sehr reich sein means 'he is said to be very rich'. The subjunctive sollte is the normal way to give advice: Du solltest mehr schlafen.

einsetzen.note: Separable verb with two very different patterns. Transitively it means 'to deploy, to use, to put into action' and takes an accusative object. Intransitively it means 'to set in, to begin' and takes no object at all. Verbs do not decline for case, so the examples show the case on the surrounding phrases.

nominative.german: Der starke Regen setzte erst am Abend ein.
nominative.english: The heavy rain only set in in the evening.
nominative.hint: Subject of setzte ... ein, so nominative; masculine nominative article der with the weak adjective ending -e. This is the intransitive use, which has no object at all.

accusative.german: Die Firma setzt seit Januar neue Maschinen ein.
accusative.english: Since January the company has been deploying new machines.
accusative.hint: Direct object of einsetzen, so accusative plural. There is no article, so the adjective takes the strong plural ending -e — identical in the nominative and accusative plural, so the verb identifies the case.

dative.german: In der neuen Abteilung wird sie als Leiterin eingesetzt.
